title: [Pulumi] AI infrastructure on tap with the Pulumi AICR provider
summary: Recently, some members of the Pulumi team spent time in San Francisco attending the CoreWeave: Fully Connected 2026 conference, where we had a chance to talk to everyone from solo developers to engineering leaders at Fortune 500 organizations and learn more about how they are building with AI. A frequent topic of conversation was open weight models and self-hosted inference. Whether AI is integrated into your platform, your product, or your productivity pipelines, rising token costs have decision makers everywhere giving open weight models a closer look, in exchange for the promise of tighter control over spend and greater domain expertise. If you are actively exploring the space or building with AI yourself, you may already have seen the challenges that come with serving inference at scale: Model stability and reliability can differ (sometimes dramatically) across hardware architectures and at different traffic volumes. Model performance and throughput can change depending on your workload type or model configuration. Cost differences and commitments across providers can make tracking spend challenging. Supply constraints and capacity shortages mean teams can’t source hardware when they need it most. Many teams naturally gravitate toward multicloud strategies that combine hyperscalers with specialized GPU clouds as a way of balancing spend, performance, and reliability. One thing we’ve seen is that developers everywhere are choosing Pulumi to help them navigate the fragmented hardware ecosystem and maintain consistent environments, even when the provider is different. As part of our ongoing commitment to building better tools for builders, we’re excited to announce the Pulumi NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) provider to help make your ideal self-hosted AI infrastructure available on demand. The Pulumi AICR provider lets you spin up workload-specific training and inference endpoints as you need them, configured with pre-validated recipes to match your workload with the right hardware across a number of cloud-based GPU providers. AI performance-engineering team as code Deploying a cluster of GPU nodes as a production AI platform is a complex and time-consuming exercise that often requires specialized expertise. NVIDIA’s AICR offers a collection of validated GPU infrastructure recipes for various cloud providers. By building a provider around AICR, Pulumi offers an efficient and reliable way to manage your GPU clusters, dramatically shortening time to first token. In addition to bundling a complex technology stack, Pulumi makes it simple to deploy with minimal verbosity. pulumi preview shows every component the recipe expands into (namespaces, operators, schedulers, metrics, training runtime) before anything is applied. pulumi up then deploys them as children of a single resource, with a full day-2 lifecycle: diff, update, drift detection, and destroy. This short Python snippet shows how easy it is to use AICR to deploy a simple pre-validated inference endpoint without wasting time or resources on guess-and-check configuration, so you can get started serving production traffic immediately. import pulumi import pulumi_labs_nvidia_aicr as aicr config = pulumi.Config() service = config.get("service") or "lke" accelerator = config.get("accelerator") or "rtx-pro-6000" # The CoreWeave Kubernetes Service (CKS) kubeconfig is a plain token config downloaded # from the CoreWeave console and placed in the same directory as this script (gitignored). with open("kubeconfig.yaml") as f: kubeconfig = f.read() gpu_stack = aicr.ClusterStack("nvidia-aicr", kubeconfig=pulumi.Output.secret(kubeconfig), accelerator=accelerator, service=service, intent="inference", nodes=2, skip_components=, skip_await=True, ) Deploying an inference endpoint to CoreWeave with the Pulumi NVIDIA AICR provider Behind the scenes, the recipe resolves the code into the full list of Kubernetes components. Recipes are tested and validated by NVIDIA across a broad matrix of both hardware (EKS, GKE, and AKS; A100 through GB200; Ubuntu, RHEL, COS, and Talos; Kubeflow, NIM, Dynamo, Slurm, and Run:ai) and cloud provider permutations. Because AICR is open source, the SDK lends itself to configuration by new providers, giving you a future-forward inference solution that performs in all of the areas that count: Deployment: does the running cluster match the recipe? Operator health, GPU visibility via nvidia-smi, and metrics flowing. Conformance: dynamic resource allocation, gang scheduling, and job-level networking behave as required. Performance: NCCL all-reduce bandwidth for training; model throughput and latency for inference. Interested in learning more about how Pulumi can help you scale your AI infrastructure? Join the Pulumi Community Slack and the hundreds of builders there, and get help crafting your dream infrastructure today.

title: [Docker] ActiveState Partners with Docker to Secure the Open Source in Enterprise Containers
summary: Even security teams that have invested in a hardened base image often can’t say what’s running on top of it. In a recent survey of 250 North American DevSecOps leaders, 91% named visibility into container components as their single biggest blind spot. Not the base image, but everything layered onto it. And 90% said their teams still run lightly modified public images with little to no hardening. That gap is getting harder to ignore. AI coding assistants are adding dependencies faster than teams can review them. Vulnerability databases can no longer keep pace with the volume of submissions. New regulatory requirements, including the EU Cyber Resilience Act, are also increasing expectations around vulnerability handling, remediation, and software supply chain transparency. Docker Hardened Images meet ActiveState’s Curated Catalog Docker, Inc. and ActiveState today announced a reselling partnership that brings Docker Hardened Images (DHI) together with ActiveState’s curated open source packages, giving enterprises a more consistent way to secure both the container base and the software dependencies layered on top. DHI provides secure-by-default, minimal container images, with 4,000+ images built from source, near-zero CVEs, signed SBOMs, and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance. The catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, with production tiers backed by a 7-day SLA for critical and high-severity CVEs. ActiveState extends that trusted foundation to the open source dependencies developers add on top. Its curated components span more than a dozen language ecosystems, including Python, JavaScript, Java, Perl, Tcl, and Ruby. Components are built from source, continuously maintained and remediated against contractual SLAs, and delivered through the package managers, pipelines, IDEs, and AI coding tools development teams already use. Trust across the software stack A more consistent approach to trusted open source: Pair a hardened container base with curated open source dependencies, reducing the need to source and manage each layer separately Verifiable provenance across the stack: With both Docker and ActiveState building from source to SLSA Build Level 3 standards, teams get a more consistent evidence trail across the software supply chain Fewer vulnerabilities, without slowing teams down : DHI delivers near-zero CVEs, 95% smaller attack surface, 7-day SLA on critical/high CVEs. ActiveState provides 95% fewer CVEs and 90% faster remediation than community open source, backed by a 5-day SLA on critical vulnerabilities. title: [HashiCorp] Banking at machine speed: Securing access across cloud, AI, and hybrid environments
summary: Banks have long invested in identity and access management to protect critical systems, customer data, and financial transactions. But cloud adoption, automation, and AI are changing who and what requires access.Applications, workloads, services and AI-enabled systems all need access to banking resources. As these environments become more distributed and automated, security leaders must maintain control without adding persistent credentials, fragmented policies, or governance gaps.What security teams are facing today goes beyond managing a growing number of identities. They must determine what autonomous systems can access, which actions they can perform, and how those activities are monitored as operations move at machine speed.How can financial institutions manage access across cloud, AI, and hybrid environments while supporting compliance, auditability, and operational resilience?Identity is becoming a governance challengeModern banking depends on automation. Applications interact with databases and cloud services. Infrastructure is provisioned dynamically. Fraud detection platforms analyze transactions in real time. AI-enabled systems may need access to transaction platforms, fraud detection services, customer data sources, and operational workflows, creating new access-control and governance considerations.A recurring theme during the recent AI Governance for Banking: Securing Agentic AI at Scale roundtable was the need for clearer controls around AI decision-making. As AI agents gain access to more systems and data, the focus shifts to defining what they should be authorized to do. That requires policies, accountability, and oversight that support regulatory compliance and AI risk management. Each workload, application, and service requires access to resources, and every request must be authenticated, authorized, and governed. As machine identities spread across public cloud, private cloud, and on-premises infrastructure, security teams need controls that can work consistently across environments. The real concern is how credentials are created, distributed, and used at machine speed, often across systems that span multiple teams, tools, and environments. Where credential risk accumulatesApplications rely on secrets, tokens, certificates, and credentials to connect with databases, APIs, and infrastructure services. Over time, these credentials can become dispersed across tools and environments, creating long-lived access, fragmented controls, and visibility gaps.Security teams need to know where credentials reside, what’s using them, and whether the access is still required. They must also provide evidence that access to critical systems is controlled, monitored, and auditable. Agents may interact with multiple systems, APIs, and data sources to complete a task. Without strong identity controls, organizations can struggle to understand what authority has been delegated, how access is being used, and whether activity remains aligned to policy.For organizations investing in banking automation, access governance now extends beyond employees and contractors. Machine identity, nonhuman identity security, secrets management, and credential management are becoming core requirements for securing AI agents, APIs, and automated workflows. As AI adoption grows in banking, reducing credential sprawl and strengthening API security are becoming important elements of a broader AI governance framework. Govern access across hybrid environmentsFor security leaders, machine identity management is both a security responsibility and governance requirement. Access policies must work across cloud and on-premises environments, even as workloads change and infrastructure scales.A centralized, policy-based approach gives teams a consistent way to authenticate machine identities, issue time-limited credentials, apply least-privilege policies, and preserve an auditable record of access activity across environments.Banks preparing for wider AI adoption will need these controls in place long before large-scale autonomous operations become commonplace.Roundtable participants emphasized that AI initiatives require the same level of oversight, policy enforcement, and accountability already expected of other critical banking systems. That visibility must extend from identity assignment and model interactions through API access and execution. Those capabilities support AI compliance, cloud governance, and operational resilience while improving visibility into autonomous activity. The case for identity-based securityIdentity-based security changes how access is granted. Instead of using a static credential stored in an application or configuration file, a workload authenticates with a verified identity. Policy determines what it can access, and a credential can be issued for a specific purpose and a limited period. This model can help financial institutions:Reduce credential and access riskApply least-privilege access more consistentlyLimit reliance on persistent credentialsMaintain a clearer, auditable record of access activityImprove machine identity and service account managementProtect the credentials behind open banking and partner APIsSupport regulatory compliance and operational resilience objectivesConsistent controls can reduce credential-management overhead and simplify governance of sensitive access across cloud, on-premises, and hybrid environments.Solutions like Vault enable this model by authenticating machine identities and issuing dynamic, policy-based credentials rather than relying on static secrets.Prepare for agentic AIAgentic AI brings added urgency to an issue banks already face. As autonomous systems take on more operational tasks, access decisions increasingly occur without direct human involvement. Governing that activity requires organizations to verify identity, limit authority, enforce policy, and maintain auditable records of access at runtime.During the AI Governance for Banking discussion, speakers noted that successful AI adoption depends on more than model performance. Organizations need operational discipline, visibility across workflows, enforceable controls, and clear ownership of outcomes. These capabilities are critical as banks address AI risk management objectives, Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) compliance initiatives, and hybrid cloud security requirements.Vault, together with the IBM® Agent Identity capability, gives banks the foundation to run AI agents safely across hybrid cloud environments. Agent Identity registers each agent and ties its delegated authority to a human user. Vault turns that delegated authority into identity-based access, issuing dynamic, short-lived secrets scoped to least privilege and capturing every request in a complete audit trail. Every action traces back to an accountable person, and access can be revoked at the source the moment something looks wrong.The solution supports the outcomes security leaders are accountable for: stronger governance, improved auditability, reduced operational burden, and greater confidence in access controls as banking infrastructure becomes more automated.Learn more about VaultBanking infrastructure is becoming increasingly automated, prompting many institutions to reassess how machine identities, secrets, and access policies are governed.Many organizations are also evaluating how AI governance, AI compliance, cloud governance, and resilience requirements fit within wider security and risk-management strategies.Explore how financial institutions are approaching risk remediation, open banking API security, nonhuman identity governance, and secure AI adoption with financial services risk remediation.Explore risk remediation strategiesRelated ContentFrom zero trust to continuous trust: Securing autonomous AI systems4/21/2026 | HashiCorp

title: [Kubernetes] Kubernetes v1.37: Tracking When a PersistentVolumeClaim Was Last Used (Beta)
summary: Kubernetes v1.37 promotes the PersistentVolumeClaimUnusedSinceTime feature gate to Beta (enabled by default). With this feature, the PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) protection controller adds an Unused condition to each PVC, telling you whether any running pod currently references it — no custom tooling or cross-referencing required. For the API definition of PVC conditions, see the PersistentVolumeClaim API reference. Read on to learn how the Unused condition works and how to use it. Why track PVC usage?In large-scale Kubernetes clusters, it is common for users to create PVCs and then delete the associated pods without cleaning up the storage, because Kubernetes does not automatically delete PVCs when their pods are removed (to protect against accidental data loss). Over time, these orphaned PVCs may accumulate, silently consuming storage capacity and driving up cloud costs. Before Kubernetes v1.37, it was easy to identify an unused PersistentVolume, but much harder to determine whether a PVC was still being used. Doing so required cross-referencing pods, PersistentVolumes, and PVCs over a potentially large window of time. Administrators often resorted to custom monitoring pipelines or scripts to answer a seemingly simple question: "Is anything actually using this volume?" The PersistentVolumeClaimUnusedSinceTime feature solves this by making the answer available natively in the PVC status. Once the feature is enabled, every PVC gets an Unused condition managed by the PVC protection controller. User stories Storage administrator: "I want to know which PVCs in my cluster are not being used by any pod so I can safely identify orphaned volumes and schedule them for deletion." DevOps engineer: "I want to list PVCs that have the Unused condition set to True so I can automate cleanup in development environments." How does it work?The PVC protection controller — which already watches pods to enforce the storage object in use protection — now also manages a new Unused condition on PVCs. The condition works as follows: Scenario Condition status Reason No non-terminal pods reference the PVC Unused=True NoPodsUsingPVC At least one running or pending pod references the PVC Unused=False PodUsingPVC A few details worth noting: Terminated pods don't count: A pod that has completed (phase Succeeded or Failed) does not keep the PVC marked as in use. This means batch jobs with restartPolicy: Never won't prevent the PVC from becoming Unused=True after they finish. Pending pods do count: Even an unschedulable pod (for example, one with an impossible node selector) still counts as using the PVC. The intent to use the volume is enough. Multiple pods: If several pods reference the same PVC, the condition transitions to Unused=True only after the *last" non-terminated pod is removed or terminates. Using lastTransitionTime to find when a PVC became idleLike every Kubernetes condition, the Unused condition carries a standard lastTransitionTime field. This means you get a useful bonus for free: when the condition transitions from False to True, the lastTransitionTime records exactly when the PVC became idle. You can use this timestamp to answer questions like "how long has this PVC been sitting unused?" — for example, to find PVCs that have been idle for more than 30 days (see the example query below). What changed from Alpha to Beta?Kubernetes v1.36 introduced this feature as Alpha, where you had to enable the PersistentVolumeClaimUnusedSinceTime feature gate explicitly. For Beta in v1.37, the feature gate is enabled by default, and the feature has full end-to-end test coverage. How to use itSince the feature is Beta and enabled by default in Kubernetes v1.37, the Unused condition will appear on PVCs automatically. Here is a walkthrough to see it in action: Create a PVC: apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: name: my-data spec: accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce resources: requests: storage: 1Gi After a short time, inspect the PVC conditions: kubectl get pvc my-data -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}' | jq . You should see an Unused condition with status True and reason NoPodsUsingPVC: { "lastProbeTime": null, "lastTransitionTime": "2026-09-14T12:03:11Z", "message": "No pods are currently referencing this PVC", "reason": "NoPodsUsingPVC", "status": "True", "type": "Unused" } Create a pod that uses the PVC: apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: my-app spec: containers: - name: app image: busybox command:  volumeMounts: - name: data mountPath: /data volumes: - name: data persistentVolumeClaim: claimName: my-data Check the condition again — it should now show Unused=False: kubectl get pvc my-data -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions.status}' Output: False Delete the pod and wait for the condition to transition back to Unused=True: kubectl delete pod my-app kubectl get pvc my-data -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}' The condition should show Unused=True with reason NoPodsUsingPVC again. Finding unused PVCs across the clusterTo list all PVCs that have been unused for more than 30 days, you can use a command like: Note:This command uses jq, a command-line JSON processor. kubectl get pvc -A -o json | jq -r ' .items | select(.status.conditions? | select(.type=="Unused" and .status=="True")) | select( (.status.conditions | select(.type=="Unused") | .lastTransitionTime) as $t | (now - ($t | fromdateiso8601)) > (30 * 86400) ) | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name) unused since \(.status.conditions | select(.type=="Unused") | .lastTransitionTime)" ' What's next?Depending on feedback and adoption, the Kubernetes project intends to graduate this feature to General Availability (GA) in a future release. If you have feedback on this feature, please open an issue in the kubernetes/kubernetes repository. To learn more about this enhancement, refer to KEP-5541: PersistentVolumeClaim last used time. Getting involvedThe Kubernetes project always welcomes new contributors. If you would like to get involved, you can join us at SIG Storage. If you would like to share feedback, you can do so on our public Slack channel (visit https://slack.k8s.io/ for an invitation if you need one). title: [CNCF] How AI workloads are reshaping Kubernetes autoscaling
summary: Kubernetes has quietly run much of the world’s containerized software on a division of labor between two control loops that rarely had to talk to each other. The scheduler places each pod on a node that already exists; the autoscaler adds nodes when pods have nowhere to fit. For a decade that separation was a sound design, because compute was largely interchangeable and either loop could work without knowing much about the other’s decisions. AI workloads, and the accelerators they run on, changed the terms; the clean split still serves most work well, and the pace of AI is what makes its edges worth revisiting. It surfaces in a situation anyone running GPUs will recognize. A pod that should schedule simply will not, even though the cluster is not truly out of capacity, and the delay can leave costly accelerator capacity unused. The instinct is to assume the region has run dry, and sometimes it has. In other cases, the capacity is available and the pod still stays pending, because the node the autoscaler is willing to add is not one the scheduler is willing to use. The autoscaler answers the question it was built for, whether to add a node, when the real question is whether that node is even the right shape for the work. The rest of this piece examines how the community has closed part of it, how it plans to close the rest, and how the autoscaler is likely to grow into a more scheduler-aware partner. The hard problems, and how the community is answering them Several of the challenges accelerators bring share a thread. Each is something both loops now have to understand the same way. Not all are new or unique to AI; some were long familiar to high-performance and batch computing, and accelerators made them everyone’s problem. Three show how far the shared answers have come. Reservations, capacity committed before the work arrives This one is the most familiar. Because supply is tight and idle accelerators are expensive, teams may reserve capacity ahead of demand. When a scale-up draws from a reservation, the autoscaler must consider not only whether to grow but also whether the resulting node uses capacity the team has already committed to and is paying for. Reservations are not an autoscaling invention. They are a long-standing capacity practice that an autoscaler may need to account for, because a node can be launched against committed capacity rather than relying on unreserved supply. Topology, the interconnect between devices, not just their count Topology is about how devices are wired to one another, not simply how far apart they sit. An accelerator leans on the parts that feed it, including the CPU and memory in its local NUMA domain, the network interface that shares its PCIe path, and the high-bandwidth links to its peer accelerators; it runs best when those pieces share a locality so traffic does not cross a slower hop. That locality is a hierarchy, from devices on the same bus inside a server, to servers in a rack joined by a fast accelerator fabric, to racks linked across a data-center network, each tier a step slower than the one beneath it. The largest models span many servers at once, so “keep these close” reaches well beyond a single node. Historically, Kubernetes commonly represented accelerator resources as counts and lacked a portable, structured way to express many device relationships; a node advertised a number, a pod asked for some, and the scheduler matched the two integers. Dynamic Resource Allocation supplies what was missing. Instead of a bare count, a workload files a structured claim describing what it needs, including a relationship like an accelerator together with the network interface that feeds it. The scheduler reads those claims directly, and DRA-aware autoscalers are starting to use the same information when they simulate capacity, though support still varies by implementation. The cost of a blind boundary. A DRA-aware autoscaler can account for a topology claim when selecting capacity; without that support it may provision an incompatible node. Sharing, putting a whole device to work, not part of it A modern accelerator is powerful enough that handing an entire one to a small job wastes most of it, so a single device can be partitioned into isolated instances that run concurrently. Some runtimes also time-slice devices, but that is a separate execution mechanism and not what consumable capacity models. Partitionable devices let one device be offered as smaller slices on demand, and consumable capacity goes finer, letting several workloads each draw a measured portion, so a request can be satisfied by a fraction of a device rather than requiring an entire device. The scheduler tracks those allocations directly, and DRA-aware autoscalers are starting to use the same model when they weigh a prospective node, though support still varies. Finer slicing can leave leftover fragments, but sensible minimum and step sizes help keep that smaller than the all-or-nothing waste it replaced. Efficiency moved inside the device. Partitioning splits one device into isolated fixed instances; consumable capacity lets several claims draw measured shares at once.Topology and sharing matter most for what they share. Together, DRA and its extensions give the scheduler and the autoscaler the same language for hardware, so the two are far less likely to disagree about what a viable node even looks like. That shared vocabulary is real progress, and it is also where the next problem begins. Why a shared vocabulary is not enough A common language lets the two loops agree on what a node is; it does not make them act as one, and some problems need exactly that. The clearest is gang scheduling, an all-or-nothing case that is not new but has grown far more acute under AI and tight capacity. A large job needs every pod to be scheduled together or none at all, and this is where shared facts alone fall short. This part is being addressed, but only on one side. Through workload-aware scheduling, whose Workload and PodGroup APIs are beta upstream and remain disabled by default, the scheduler is learning to treat a group as one all-or-nothing unit, holding its pods until enough can be placed together so a half-placed job no longer strands hardware. The autoscaler was not part of that change. It still reasons pod by pod, so it can add a node or two for a few pending members of a gang and waste that capacity while the job never starts. A companion mechanism, the provisioning request, is the current bridge. It lets a workload ask the autoscaler for a whole group’s capacity at once rather than pod by pod. With a configured admission check, Kueue reserves quota, creates the request, waits for capacity to be reported ready, and then admits the workload. Atomic scale-up is best effort and depends on provider support. It remains a bolt-on across a seam rather than a shared understanding, and it points at the deeper pattern. A capable autoscaler already reasons a little like a scheduler, predicting where the scheduler would place pods to decide whether a new node would help. The clearest sign is duplicated effort already baked in. The autoscaler simulates the scheduler’s placement to decide what to launch, and once the node exists the scheduler makes its own placement decision, repeating much of the same reasoning. What the community is building next This is why the two loops, which still do different jobs, increasingly have to be designed together, and that convergence is becoming an active design discussion. The workload-aware scheduling effort has signaled that its scope is meant to reach beyond the scheduler toward autoscaling over time, and a public proposal in the SIG-Autoscaling community now sketches integration APIs that let the two speak directly. One would let the scheduler see capacity that could be provisioned rather than only the nodes already present, one would express placement preferences across it, and one would request it explicitly. The deeper motivation is process. If autoscaling is a first-class concern while a feature is designed, provisioning gets considered while a new placement primitive is taking shape rather than only after it ships, so the seam becomes something the community weighs up front rather than something autoscalers scramble to close after each release. What to take away The mental model worth keeping is one hardware model, two consumers. A scarce accelerator is only as useful as the agreement between the loop that schedules it and the loop that provisions it, and every place only one of them understands a capability is a place they can disagree and may leave costly hardware idle. So when a pod stays pending, do not assume the capacity is gone; check whether the scheduler and the autoscaler agree on what a usable node looks like. Inference is what makes this pressing rather than academic, since bursty serving and agentic workloads have no patience for a cold node. These interfaces are being drawn in the open right now, in SIG-Autoscaling and SIG-Scheduling rather than in any one vendor’s product, so anyone running accelerators has both a stake in the outcome and a chance to shape it before the design sets.

title: [Cloudflare] Cloudflare deploys protections against php2shell vulnerability
summary: Update - On October 23, the PHP project published an informational advisory for a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, in PHP's session upload progress feature. It affects fully patched PHP releases, including 8.5.12, and will be fixed in PHP's next regular release.All Cloudflare WAF customers are protected against known exploit attempts if their site uses PHP's default upload progress field name. Customers who have changed session.upload_progress.name are not covered by the WAF rule.The existing rules "PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) #6" protects against this vulnerability.More information to follow.October 21, Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI and Quarkslab disclosed two vulnerabilities in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and known as php2shell. The vulnerabilities affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later and they may allow an attacker to cause denial of service, remote code execution, and data exposure when an application processes specially crafted HTTP traffic.Cloudflare has been part of a coordinated effort to deploy mitigations to protect the Internet, working with PHP foundation, OpenAI and Wiz among others. Cloudflare has developed and deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections since early October 2026, which were deployed about 9 hours ahead of public disclosure. Starting on October 21 3:02 am UTC, Cloudflare customers using our free or paid WAF were protected by default against php2shell.Cloudflare successfully deployed multiple mitigations for all its customers while the vulnerability was leaked before the official release date and we observed attack traffic targeting our customers. We observed how attackers were mutating the attack payload to try to bypass our protections by tracking the volume of matches and cross-referencing with the rule logic.Protecting against php2shell required more than standard request-based rules. Request data alone does not always provide enough evidence to distinguish an exploit from legitimate traffic. The origin’s response adds context, helping identify whether an exploit succeeded while reducing the risk of false positives.To deliver this protection, we developed full transaction detection, a new Cloudflare WAF capability that combines signals from the request and response within the same HTTP transaction. Response rules can then block a matching origin response before it reaches the requester. The php2shell protections are the first managed detections we have released using this capability.Customers should patch their PHP repos even with WAF protections providing an additional layer of defense-in-depth mitigation. Our security analysts continue monitoring attack activity and update the rules when and if new techniques and variations emerge in the hours and days ahead. You can track new rules in the changelog.The protections are available and deployed automatically on all plans with WAF deployed, including Free users.What we know about the vulnerabilitiesPHP is used by almost 70% of websites. The php2shell vulnerabilities affect the PHP runtime itself and can allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Because PHP underpins widely used platforms such as WordPress and Magento, these flaws could potentially affect a large number of applications across the Internet.The two vulnerabilities involve how PHP handles memory when something goes wrong while processing a HTTP request. Normally, PHP allocates memory to store the data it needs to process a request, then releases it when that work finishes. If processing stops unexpectedly, for example because it runs out of memory, PHP fails to clean up the memory safely. These vulnerabilities arise when PHP handles an error and then tries to use data that was not fully set up or memory that has already been released.An attacker can send specially crafted HTTP requests to trigger these conditions. Large requests are one way to put memory under pressure, but the problem goes beyond consuming server resources. By manipulating the data PHP encounters in this invalid memory, an attacker may be able to crash a PHP process, expose sensitive information, or execute code provided by the attacker.The two vulnerabilities differ in when the unsafe memory access happens:VulnerabilityWhat goes wrongCVE-2026-109618PHP runs out of memory and interrupts its work before some internal data has been properly initialized. During cleanup of that request, PHP may use this unfinished data as though it were valid.CVE-2026-109619A fatal error interrupts a request, leaving PHP holding references to memory that is released when the request ends. When the same PHP process handles a later request, it may follow those outdated references and access memory that is no longer valid and expose sensitive data.These flaws are in the PHP runtime, so updating website code or a plugin(s) alone does not fix these vulnerabilities. Administrators need to update the PHP software running their applications. If a hosting provider manages PHP, ask the provider to apply the security update.Administrators can follow the PHP advisory for affected versions and remediation instructions. Keep Cloudflare WAF protections enabled while patching. Restricting unnecessary uploads and limiting upload sizes can also reduce exposure, but these measures do not replace the PHP fix.New rulesFor Free customers, new rules have been released under the Cloudflare Managed Free Ruleset (Ruleset ID 77454fe2d30c4220b5701f6fdfb893ba). Free customers don’t have to take any actions to enable the protection. They allow unauthenticated remote code execution, data exposure and DoS through crafted HTTP requests. Exploitation is already happening. The bug is in the PHP runtime itself, so updating app code, frameworks, WordPress or plugins does NOT fix it. Official advisory (treat as source of truth, re-fetch it in case it was updated): https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-21-5 - GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w (CVE-2026-109618, RCE via OOM corruption) - GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp (CVE-2026-109619, RCE via stale global state) **Fixed upstream versions:** 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35 **Affected:** every PHP install that serves web requests (PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed). mod_php has the highest risk: a demonstrated exploit triggers before any application code runs. ## Rules - Do NOT guess. If you can't confirm a version or setting, say so. - Ask me before changing anything on production or shared infrastructure, restarting production services, or editing deploy config. Read-only discovery is fine. - Don't stop at the first finding. Inventory everything, then report. ## Step 1: Inventory every place PHP runs Search the current repo/workspace AND any machines/containers I have access to: - Repo: `*.php`, `composer.json`/`composer.lock` (check `require.php` and `config.platform.php`), `Dockerfile*`, `docker-compose*`, `.php-version`, `.tool-versions`, `.devcontainer/`, CI files (GitHub Actions `setup-php`, GitLab CI `image:`), IaC (Terraform, Ansible, Helm, k8s manifests), PaaS config (`app.yaml`, `Procfile`, Platform.sh, Laravel Forge/Vapor, etc.). - Base images: list every `FROM php:*`, `FROM wordpress:*`, `FROM bitnami/*`, `FROM serversideup/*`, `FROM dunglas/frankenphp*` and similar, with tags. - Running hosts/containers (if accessible): `php -v`, `php-fpm -v`, `php -i | grep -i "server api"`, `apachectl -M | grep -i php`, `docker ps` + `docker exec <c> php -v`. - Note the SAPI for each (FPM / mod_php / CGI / FrankenPHP / LiteSpeed / CLI-only). - Note long-running workers (Laravel Octane, RoadRunner, Swoole, FrankenPHP worker mode). These are relevant to the stale-state bug. If no PHP is found anywhere, tell me clearly and stop. Nothing else is needed. ## Step 2: Decide if each instance is vulnerable For each instance, classify it as PATCHED / VULNERABLE / UNKNOWN: - Upstream builds: vulnerable if below 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35 on that branch. - **PHP 8.1 and older are EOL upstream:** vulnerable unless a vendor backport is confirmed. - **Distro packages (Debian/Ubuntu/RHEL/Alpine/etc.)** often backport fixes WITHOUT bumping the upstream version, so `php -v` alone isn't enough. Check the package changelog for the CVE IDs, e.g. `apt changelog <php-pkg> | grep -E "CVE-2026-10961"` or `rpm -q --changelog <php-pkg> | grep -E "CVE-2026-10961"`. - If PHP comes from `rpms.remirepo.net`: the advisory says it will not have same-day updates. Flag this and recommend distro packages or building from source. - Managed hosting / shared hosting / PaaS: mark UNKNOWN and tell me to ask the provider. ## Step 3: Fix (only after I approve the plan for prod) 1. Upgrade PHP to a fixed version (or the vendor-patched package): - Bump Docker base image tags to a fixed patch release, rebuild, redeploy. - Update CI `php-version` pins. - `apt`/`dnf`/`apk` upgrade of the distro PHP packages. - 7.4 / 8.0 / 8.1 built from source: the PHP security team published minimal backport branches linked from the advisory. Otherwise upgrade to a supported version. 2. **Restart EVERY PHP worker** (FPM pools, Apache, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed, Octane/ RoadRunner/Swoole). Old processes keep running vulnerable code until restarted. 3. Verify each instance afterwards (version + changelog check) and report the evidence. ## Step 4: Temporary mitigations (ONLY if patching isn't possible right away) These reduce exposure but do NOT make the server safe. Apply them in php.ini / the FPM pool / server config (not `ini_set()` or `.user.ini`) and restart every worker: - CVE-2026-109618: - `memory_limit=-1`, set non-overridably (e.g. `php_admin_value`), and confirm nothing re-applies a finite limit. - Low `post_max_size` (8M with no uploads, 32M with uploads), with `upload_max_filesize` below it. - Enforce request size / field count / multipart part count / header limits at the web server or proxy, including requests without `Content-Length`. - Use container/cgroup memory limits. Do NOT use `RLIMIT_AS`/`RLIMIT_DATA`. - CVE-2026-109619: - `session.upload_progress.enabled=0`. - On PHP 8.5: `fatal_error_backtraces=0`. - Remove invalid/deprecated per-request settings that emit diagnostics early (hiding them via `error_reporting`/`display_errors`/`@` does not help). - Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and timeouts. - If the site sits behind Cloudflare: confirm the WAF Managed Ruleset is deployed in **block** mode (Free plans get the Managed Free Ruleset automatically). This is defense in depth, not a replacement for patching. ## Step 5: Look for signs of compromise (read-only) Since exploitation started before disclosure, check what you can access: - PHP-FPM/Apache error logs for segfaults, "Allowed memory size exhausted", or worker crashes, especially clustered around unusually large POST/multipart requests. - Recently modified or unexpected files in web roots (webshells), new cron jobs, unexpected processes or outbound connections from PHP users. Report anything suspicious. Do not delete evidence. ## Final report Give me a table: location | how PHP is provided | SAPI | version | status (PATCHED/VULNERABLE/UNKNOWN) | action taken or needed. Then list: - What you changed (files, commands), what still needs my approval, and anything that needs a hosting provider. - Mitigations applied as stopgaps and when they should be removed. - Any compromise indicators found.

title: [Slack Engineering] From SSH to REST: A Security-Driven Modernization of Slack’s EMR Data Pipelines
summary: Excerpt By 2024, Slack’s data platform had accumulated 700+ SSH-based operators orchestrating critical data pipelines. We’re talking daily search indexing that processed terabytes of data, analytics jobs powering business intelligence, the whole shebang. Every single one of these jobs required direct SSH access to production AWS Elastic MapReduce (EMR) clusters. We had a massive security surface, and we couldn’t move forward on any infrastructure modernization. Not ideal. We needed to eliminate SSH entirely. The solution? Migrate all 700+ jobs to a REST-based architecture. This is the story of how we killed SSH entirely, across 8 data regions, with zero downtime. How We Got Here Slack’s data platform was built around 2017 with a straightforward pattern. Airflow, our data pipeline orchestrator, needed to run jobs on EMR clusters, and SSH was the most direct path. Connect to the EMR master node, execute a command, done. Simple. # The old way - simple, but problematic task = SSHOperator( task_id='run_spark_job', ssh_conn_id='emr_master', command='spark-submit /path/to/job.py', ) This pattern proliferated across the platform. Teams built custom SSH-based operators for different use cases (because hey, if SSH works for Spark, why not everything else). By the time we took stock, we had 700+ jobs in production running everything from MapReduce jobs to AWS CLI commands to custom Python scripts. It worked. But it came with some potential problems. The Real Cost of SSH Potential security risks included: Direct SSH access to compute clusters increases the potential attack surface Key distribution and rotation across orchestration workers adds operational overhead Achieving fine-grained audit granularity typically requires correlating logs across multiple systems Permission management can grow complex, often requiring dedicated security groups and custom configurations Operations were painful: Jobs ran directly on EMR master nodes instead of being distributed, causing resource contention When Kubernetes pods restarted, SSH connections broke and jobs failed Long-running jobs became “zombies” that kept executing after their connections terminated No reliable way to determine if a job succeeded or failed when connections dropped (not ideal when you’re processing terabytes) We were blocked: Couldn’t start the path for Spark on Kubernetes nor EMR on AWS Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) (required eliminating SSH dependencies first) Couldn’t complete our Whitecastle initiative because we needed to move the last main-account EMR clusters to child accounts Whitecastle is Slack’s initiative to migrate AWS infrastructure to child accounts for improved security and network isolation. Building the Next Evolution of Cloud Networks at Slack: A Retrospective Couldn’t implement proper job monitoring and observability An example problem: The Search Infrastructure team’s pipeline builds Solr search indexes from terabytes of data daily. This pipeline powers Slack’s search functionality. Any disruption affects search quality for millions of users. And it was relying on SSH-based job submission with all the reliability problems mentioned above. Not great. Understanding the Foundation: REST-Based Job Submission Before diving into the solution, let’s establish what REST-based job submission actually means (and why it matters). The Problem with SSH When you SSH into a machine and run a command, you’re creating a direct, stateful connection. If that connection drops (say your Kubernetes pod restarts), the command might keep running, might fail, or might leave orphaned processes hanging around. You’ve got no reliable way to reconnect and check status. It’s like hanging up mid-phone call and hoping the other person finishes the conversation. The REST Alternative Modern compute engines (YARN, Trino, Snowflake) expose HTTP APIs for job submission. Instead of maintaining a connection, you: POST a job request → receive a job ID GET job status using the ID → check if it’s running, completed, or failed DELETE the job → cleanly cancel, if needed The job lifecycle is managed server-side. Your client can crash and restart, and the job keeps running while you can still query its status. Much better. The YARN Piece For Hadoop workloads (MapReduce, Spark, Hive), YARN is the resource manager with a REST API for job submission. But here’s the catch: YARN’s API is designed for Hadoop jobs. What about the 300+ CLI-based jobs running arbitrary shell commands like aws s3 sync or hadoop distcp? That’s where YARN Distributed Shell comes in. This was the key breakthrough that made this whole migration possible. The Breakthrough: YARN Distributed Shell Migrating Spark and Hive jobs was more straightforward. Spark has the Livy REST API and Hive has HiveServer2. But MapReduce jobs and the 300+ CLI-based jobs running arbitrary shell commands? Those were the hard parts. They didn’t have ready-made REST APIs. We brainstormed multiple approaches. Our requirements were clear: Simple REST-based solution: fits naturally into our architecture Existing authentication and authorization mechanisms: no custom security layer to build and maintain Open-source protocols: leverage standard YARN APIs, not proprietary solutions Minimal complexity: no building and maintaining custom job execution infrastructure Some ideas we considered: Building a custom wrapper service to execute commands remotely Using remote execution frameworks like Ansible or Salt Creating a new job type in YARN from scratch All of these felt too complex, required custom security implementations, or introduced new dependencies we’d have to maintain. Not great options. Then we discovered YARN’s Distributed Shell. It’s a little-known feature (org.apache.hadoop.yarn.applications.distributedshell.ApplicationMaster) that allows any shell script to run in a proper YARN container with resource allocation and lifecycle management. And here’s the kicker: it was already part of YARN, used the same REST APIs, and required no custom security layer. It was perfect. Here’s how it works: 1. Upload your command to S3 For example, we could upload the following script (command.sh) to s3://bucket/ # command.sh aws s3 sync /tmp/data/ s3://bucket/output/ 2. Submit to YARN with Distributed Shell configuration { "application-type": "MAPREDUCE", "am-container-spec": { "commands": { "command": "{{JAVA_HOME}}/bin/java org.apache.hadoop.yarn.applications.distributedshell.ApplicationMaster ..." }, "environment": { "DISTRIBUTEDSHELLSCRIPTLOCATION": "s3://bucket/command.sh", "DISTRIBUTEDSHELLSCRIPTLEN": "548", "DISTRIBUTEDSHELLSCRIPTTIMESTAMP": "1768529627000" } } } 3. YARN allocates a container, downloads the script, and executes it: Yarn manages: Proper resource limits (memory, vCores) Container isolation Retry and fault tolerance Clean cancellation Proper logging through YARN UI This architectural decision unlocked the migration of all SSH-based jobs. Not just Hadoop workloads, but any shell command. Whether it was aws s3 sync, hadoop distcp, or custom Python scripts, they could all run in proper YARN containers. Game changer. Figure 1: YARN Distributed Shell job submission flow showing how arbitrary shell commands are executed in YARN containers through Quarry. The Solution: Quarry Now that we understand the advantages of REST-based job submission and how we can migrate each existing job type, we’re just missing one thing: an orchestrator. Enter Quarry, Slack’s REST-based job submission gateway. Quarry was originally built to provide a unified interface for submitting jobs across multiple compute engines (EMR/YARN, Trino, Snowflake). It already solved authentication, reliability, and observability challenges. For SSH deprecation, it turned out to be exactly what we needed. What Quarry Does Quarry sits between various services and compute engines (Airflow being the biggest user), handling: Authentication: Service-to-service tokens instead of SSH keys Job submission: REST APIs to YARN, Trino, and Snowflake State tracking: Server-side monitoring of job status Lifecycle management: Clean cancellation and cleanup through REST APIs Observability: Structured logs, metrics, and tracing for all job submissions The Architecture Shift Before: Airflow → SSH Connection → EMR Master Node → Execute Command After: Airflow → Quarry REST API → YARN ResourceManager → EMR Container Instead of establishing SSH connections, Airflow operators make HTTP requests to Quarry. Quarry submits jobs to YARN and polls for status. If an Airflow pod restarts, the job keeps running, and Quarry maintains the connection. Figure 2: Architecture comparison showing the shift from SSH-based direct execution to REST-based job submission through Quarry and YARN. The Quarry Advantage With YARN Distributed Shell support, Quarry became our universal job submission gateway. Whether you’re running a Spark job, a Hive query, or a simple shell script, it all goes through the same REST API. No SSH credentials. No direct cluster access. Just REST API calls with proper authentication and server-side job tracking. The Migration Journey We knew from the start this wasn’t going to be a quick fix. We had 700+ production jobs across 8 independent data regions, each with unique network configurations and data sovereignty requirements. Critical workloads, like search indexing, couldn’t tolerate any downtime. So yeah, we needed a plan. The Approach: Incremental and Phased Phase 1 – Proof of Concept: Started with pilot jobs to validate the Quarry-based approach. Built the first Quarry operators and tested in dev environments. Phase 2 – Security Review: Engaged security teams to plan credential elimination and ensure the REST-based approach met security requirements. Phase 3 – OKR-Driven Execution: Made it a Key Result with executive visibility. This created accountability and kept it prioritized. We hit the 80% migration milestone during this phase. Phase 4 – Bulk Migration: Heavy cross-team coordination to migrate remaining workloads across all regions. Multiple teams (Search Infrastructure, Data Engineering & Analytics, ML Services) worked in parallel. Phase 5 – Final Cleanup: Completed overlooked DAGs and deprecated all legacy SSH-based operators. Achieved 100% completion. Migration by the Numbers 700+ jobs migrated across 7 operator types 8 independent data regions with coordinated rollouts 5 teams transitioned to new operators Zero downtime for business-critical services Completed in 3 quarters, from initial pilot to 100% SSH elimination The Challenges We Hit No migration this size goes smoothly. Here are the biggest obstacles we ran into (and how we dealt with them). Challenge 1: Virtual Memory Check Failures During migration of a data export DAG, we hit unexpected failures. Jobs that’d been running fine via SSH were now failing with vmem (virtual memory) check errors. What gives? The root cause: SSH commands ran directly on the master node, bypassing YARN’s resource enforcement entirely. Quarry submits jobs properly to YARN, which actually enforces resource limits. The vmem check was rejecting containers that exceeded virtual memory limits (which SSH had been quietly ignoring). The fix: Following AWS best practices, we disabled vmem checks across all clusters: "yarn.nodemanager.vmem-check-enabled": "false" AWS explicitly recommends this because virtual memory accounting in Linux can be unreliable, and physical memory limits are sufficient. (Also, it’s worth noting that vmem checks have been a source of spurious failures for years in the Hadoop ecosystem.) Lesson learned: When migrating from SSH to proper YARN submission, expect to encounter resource limit issues that were previously invisible. SSH hides a lot of problems. Test thoroughly in dev environments before production rollout. Challenge 2: Network Segregation and EKM Connectivity During migration of dev search infrastructure jobs from one dev cluster to a staging analytics cluster, a task failed with an EKM (Enterprise Key Management) connectivity timeout. Great. Error: com.amazon.ws.emr.hadoop.fs.shaded.com.amazonaws.SdkClientException: Unable to execute HTTP request: Connect to sts.amazonaws.com:443 failed: connect timed out The root cause: the original cluster had network routing configured to reach the necessary key management endpoints. The staging analytics cluster, operating in a stricter network segment, did not have equivalent connectivity and correctly so. The failure surfaced a hidden dependency on network topology that wasn’t captured in the job’s configuration. The fix: We moved search infrastructure tasks to a dev ETL cluster with proper routing to dev services. For tasks requiring production Hive catalogs, we kept them in staging. We also scaled up the dev ETL cluster to handle the additional workload. Lesson learned: Network topology matters. Like, really matters. Understand network segregation and account boundaries before deciding which cluster runs which jobs. Dev jobs need dev network access, prod jobs need prod network access. The migration revealed hidden dependencies that SSH had been quietly papering over. Challenge 3: Multi-Region Complexity Slack operates EMR clusters across 8 independent data regions to support data sovereignty requirements. This meant the SSH deprecation wasn’t a single migration. It was effectively 8 parallel migrations, each with its own special set of challenges. Fun times. The Complexity Configuration management: Each region required separate Quarry configurations, cluster endpoints, and network routing rules Testing overhead: Every code change needed validation across all 8 regions before production rollout (multiply your testing time by 8) Staggered deployments: Couldn’t deploy to all regions simultaneously. Had to roll out region by region. Region-specific issues: Network configurations, data sovereignty rules, and cluster versions varied by region Our Approach Validated changes in a single pilot region (typically US-based for faster iteration) Documented region-specific configuration requirements Built region-aware Quarry operators that could handle regional differences Rolled out to remaining regions incrementally, learning from each deployment Maintained separate tracking for each region’s migration progress Lesson learned: Multi-region infrastructure significantly multiplies migration complexity. The effort isn’t just N times harder. It’s N times harder with unique failure modes for each region. Budget extra time for cross-region coordination and region-specific debugging. (Seriously, budget more time than you think.) The Results We achieved 100% SSH elimination. Every production job now runs through Quarry with REST-based submission. Here’s what we gained. Security Wins Eliminated SSH access to all production EMR clusters across 8 independent data regions, which massively reduced our attack surface. We replaced SSH key distribution with service-to-service token authentication, and gained proper audit trails through REST API logging. Every job submission now has structured logs through Quarry. No more “who ran that command?” mysteries. This also enabled completion of our Whitecastle initiative by allowing us to migrate the last AWS main account EMR cluster to a child account. Bonus: we simplified compliance by removing special security group configurations and the complex permission management that SSH access required. Operational Improvements Master node resource contention: eliminated. All non-Hadoop jobs now run in distributed YARN containers with proper resource allocation instead of competing for resources on the master node. Job reliability: dramatically improved. Jobs survive client Kubernetes pod restarts because Quarry maintains server-side job tracking. No more zombie processes. Jobs terminate properly when cancelled through REST APIs. We gained proper lifecycle management with clean cancellation and cleanup. Observability: transformed. Structured job status, logs, and metrics are now available through Quarry’s API. We can track jobs across their entire lifecycle, see YARN container logs, and actually debug issues with proper tooling instead of SSH-ing into boxes and hoping for the best. Future Enablement The REST-based architecture unblocked critical initiatives: Spark on Kubernetes migration now possible (no SSH dependencies to migrate) Modern infrastructure patterns enabled (REST-based architecture aligns with cloud-native practices) Easier team onboarding (simpler, more maintainable Quarry operators vs. complex SSH configurations) Platform evolution (decoupled Airflow from EMR infrastructure details) Standardized job submission (consolidated all job submission through Quarry, making future changes easier) With two years of production experience since completion, the architectural decisions have proven sound. The REST-based approach delivered on its promises: better security, operational stability, and infrastructure flexibility. No regrets. What We Learned What Worked Well Incremental migration approach: Dev → GovDev/CommDev → Prod rollout minimized risk at every step. We migrated jobs by operator type rather than trying to convert everything simultaneously. This allowed us to learn from each migration and refine our approach for the next batch. Strong team collaboration: Multiple teams working together seamlessly across search, analytics, data engineering, ML, and marketing domains. Prompt code reviews kept momentum high. Regular communication in shared channels kept everyone informed. Analytics-driven progress tracking: We created an Analytics dashboard to track migration progress across all regions. Querying the Airflow database to identify remaining SSH-based tasks made it easy to see which teams/DAGs still needed migration. This data-driven approach kept the project moving. What We’d Do Differently Earlier network topology mapping: We discovered network segregation issues (like the EKM connectivity problem) pretty late in the migration. Understanding Whitecastle account boundaries and network routing upfront would’ve saved us some pain. Next time: document network topology and dependencies before starting cluster migrations. Don’t assume SSH’s simplicity means everything will “Just Work” when you swap it out. Earlier resource limit testing: The vmem check issue caught us by surprise late in the project. We should’ve tested YARN resource limits against an SSH baseline way earlier in the process. Recommendation: Include resource limit testing in the initial pilot migration phase. SSH bypasses a lot of stuff, and you want to know what that stuff is before it bites you in production. Better communication about operator restrictions: When we restricted SSHOperator to prevent new usage during the final migration phase, some teams weren’t aware. Better advance notice to all Airflow users would’ve prevented confusion and friction. Internal communication is hard, but it matters. Best Practices for Large-Scale Migrations Build monitoring before you migrate: Set up tracking dashboards early so you always know what’s left to migrate. Airflow database queries made it easy to identify remaining work. Progress visibility kept the project moving. Test in multiple environments: Dev, CommDev, and GovDev testing caught environment-specific issues before production. Network segregation issues only appeared when testing across account boundaries. Don’t skip environment-specific testing. Hidden dependencies will absolutely bite you. Progressive operator deprecation: We deprecated operators one at a time (CrunchExecOperator, then S3SyncOperator, etc.). Each deprecation was its own mini-project with testing and validation. While it was slower than migrating everything at once, it greatly mitigated the risk of the migration. Acknowledgments We wanted to give a shout out to all the people that have contributed to this journey: Gage Gaskin Deepak Agarwal And to all the teams that successfully transitioned their pipelines to the new architecture!
