title: [Lyft Engineering] Rerouting the Stream: How Lyft Moved to the Apache Flink Kubernetes Operator
summary: Written by Maheep Myneni, Arda Kuyumcu, and Prem Santosh Udaya Shankar at Lyft.Why We Migrated: Technical Debt Meets Modern Streaming DemandsOver the past several quarters, Lyft’s Streaming Compute team retired our internally developed Flink Kubernetes operator and moved our entire streaming fleet onto the open-source Apache Flink Kubernetes operator. This post is about why we made the switch, how we pulled it off incrementally without disrupting users, and the follow-on work it took to actually get the benefits we were after.Back in 2020, when we first architected the Lyft Flink Kubernetes Operator, it was exactly what we needed. At that time, the open-source community hadn’t yet built a dedicated control plane, so we built our own to manage all streaming applications on Kubernetes. It worked well for our initial workloads, but as our real-time data needs increased and our engineers’ scope of ownership grew in both breadth and complexity, the cracks started to show.First came the maintenance burden. Our operator had become a relic of Lyft’s early Kubernetes days, kept alive by a growing pile of custom code. Every Flink version upgrade meant carefully picking through layers of accumulated technical debt and hoping nothing broke on the way through.Second came the feature gap. Streaming tooling kept moving, and our engineers kept asking for capabilities that had become table stakes elsewhere, such as autoscaling to right-size jobs, automatic rollbacks on failed deploys, and an end to hand-tuning CPU and memory. Each request left us with two options, neither of which was ideal. We could explain why we couldn’t support it yet, or spend weeks rebuilding something the open-source community had already shipped.Third was the dependency problem. We were pinned to outdated libraries. That doesn’t break anything today, but it almost always creates new issues down the line. Security patches lagged, modern Kubernetes features stayed out of reach, and every quarter we waited made the eventual escape messier.Meanwhile, the Apache Flink Kubernetes Operator had matured into production-grade infrastructure, and its feature set read like our wishlist: intelligent job-vertex autoscaling to kill backpressure, automatic memory tuning, safe upgrade mechanisms, and a robust reconciliation loop. Additionally, it was battle-tested by companies at massive scale. The decision in front of us became obvious. We needed to migrate Lyft’s fleet, hundreds of critical streaming jobs, from our internal operator to the Apache one. However, we had to do this migration without disrupting existing deployment patterns, altering our team’s workflows, or causing massive outages in production.This is the story of how we pulled it off, and why sometimes the best code you can write is the code you delete.Our Legacy: The Lyft Flink Kubernetes OperatorBefore we dive into the migration itself, it’s worth understanding what we were migrating from. The Lyft Flink Kubernetes Operator served us well for years, and being familiar with its architecture helps illustrate both why the migration was necessary and why it was nontrivial.At its core, Lyft’s operator follows the standard Kubernetes pattern by continuously watching custom resources and reconciling their state. We defined Flink applications using a FlinkApplication custom resource that looked something like this:apiVersion: flink.k8s.io/v1beta1kind: FlinkApplicationmetadata: name: my-streaming-job namespace: productionspec: image: lyft/my-flink-job:v1.2.3 flinkVersion: "1.16" jarName: "my-streaming-job.jar" entryClass: "com.lyft.streaming.MyJob" parallelism: 8 jobManagerConfig: replicas: 1 resources: memory: "2048Mi" cpu: "1.0" taskManagerConfig: taskSlots: 4 resources: memory: "4096Mi" cpu: "2.0" flinkConfig: state.backend.fs.checkpointdir: s3://lyft-flink/checkpoints state.savepoints.dir: s3://lyft-flink/savepoints execution.checkpointing.interval: 60sLyft’s operator takes this spec and creates the necessary Kubernetes resources: a JobManager (JM) deployment, a TaskManager (TM) deployment, any external runtime configurations, and optionally an ingress for the Flink UI. Simple enough, in theory.The State Machine: Where Things Got InterestingThe Lyft operator’s real complexity lived in the state machine. Deploying a stateful streaming application isn’t like deploying a stateless web service; you can’t simply kill the old pods and start new ones. If you did, all in-flight data and state would be lost. Our operator walked through a careful choreography of states to ensure zero data loss.Dual Deployment Mode (our default) had minimal, but non-zero downtime. When a user updated a FlinkApplication, the operator would spin up a completely new Flink cluster alongside the running one. Once the new cluster was healthy, it would trigger a savepoint on the old job, wait for it to complete, cancel the old job, tear down the old cluster, and finally submit the job to the new cluster from the savepoint.BlueGreen Mode took it a step further for truly zero-downtime deployments. Both clusters would run simultaneously (“dual running”), and you would manually switch traffic by setting a tearDownVersionHash field after verifying the new version was working correctly. This gave users a manual kill switch, which worked well for critical jobs where one would want to inspect the new version before committing.The state machine tracked states like ClusterStarting, Savepointing, SubmittingJob, Running, DeployFailed, and our favorite debugging companion, Recovering (for when savepoints failed and we needed to fall back to externalized checkpoints). Each transition was carefully orchestrated with retry logic, timeout handling, and event logging.Problems: The Cracks in the FoundationBeyond the maintenance burden and the feature gap, two specific pain points made this decision unavoidable. Both stemmed from early design choices that suited a smaller fleet, but broke down as our workloads grew to be more varied over time.Savepoint FragilitySavepoints were the only first-class mechanism for preserving application state during upgrades. If a savepoint failed, the operator fell back to looking for an externalized checkpoint. However, the checkpoint fallback was a last-resort recovery path rather than a strategy users could deliberately choose. The savepoint trigger had no retry logic and no idempotency guarantees. If no recent checkpoint was available, the deploy either failed or restarted the job with no state at all. For large-state jobs where savepoints were slow or occasionally timed out, a transient failure escalated into a full recovery cycle. The Apache operator introduced last-state as an explicit upgrade mode, which uses high-availability metadata or the latest checkpoint by design. This was exactly the robustness we needed, particularly for jobs where an unhealthy JobManager couldn’t cooperate with a savepoint request.Rigid Resource ModelOur operator exposed a single systemMemoryFraction knob. This represented a fraction of container memory reserved for non-JVM use. For pure Flink Java applications, this overhead was often unnecessary. For Apache Beam workloads using the Python SDK harness, it was vital. Unfortunately, how much memory those Python processes actually needed was essentially guesswork, since usage happened inside the Flink memory model. There was no observability into the utilization and no way to tune it systematically. If we set it too low, TMs would get OOM-killed. If we set it too high, we wasted resources.Migration: Our Blueprint for a Seamless SwitchSetting up a new system is the easy part. The real nightmare of any migration is unwinding everything that still points to the old one. At Lyft, all Flink deployment configs start as Jsonnet files. We use a shared module to set up operational defaults, and individual teams layer their own application configs on top:common.sp.FlinkApplication("myflinkapplication", "staging", "myproject") { application+: { spec+: { parallelism: 8, flinkConfig+: { "state.backend": "filesystem", "restart-strategy.fixed-delay.delay": "10s" } } },}In the above example, an individual app extends the base factory with its own parallelism and Flink configuration. The entire system was built around the legacy operator’s FlinkApplication custom resource definition (CRD). Rewriting every library and application overlay to natively produce the Apache operator’s FlinkDeployment CRD would have been a massive and risky undertaking.Instead, we chose to translate at the boundary, so teams could continue defining their applications exactly as they always had. The translation from FlinkApplication to FlinkDeployment happens within our deploy API. When the deploy API encounters a legacy resource, it converts the resource into something the Apache operator is familiar with. This handles the structural mapping:Job Spec: We assemble flat fields like jarName and parallelism into the Apache operator’s nested spec. jarName becomes a jarURI.Upgrade Mode: We default to last-state to restore state from the last checkpoint if possible, and map legacy configs like savepointDisabled to stateless.Pod Templates: Inline container configs on the legacy spec like node selectors, tolerations, and sidecar annotations get promoted into proper PodTemplateSpec objects.Backwards Compatibility: We inject legacy environment variables like APP_NAME and HOST_NAME so application code doesn’t break.Crucially, the migration was incremental. Dynamic configuration allowed us to migrate one application at a time, starting with staging. If an app hit issues, we could instantly roll it back to the legacy operator. To the developer, the change was largely invisible.From the Trenches: Additional Work to Integrate the OperatorWhile the translation layer got us onto the Apache operator, the migration was not yet done. We still had to address a few follow-on problems, and do additional work to make sure we saw all the benefits the Apache operator had to offer. Two of those benefits are autoscaling, which dynamically adjusts a job’s parallelism, and autotuning, which adjusts the memory resources each TaskManager gets.BlueGreen DeploymentsOnce we migrated apps onto the Apache operator, every deploy cost us an average of 3–6 minutes of downtime, and closer to 20 minutes for our largest jobs. Lyft’s operator had managed JobManager and TaskManager lifecycles together through a complex graph of operations, which kept downtime to a minimum. The Apache operator took a different approach; it spun up only the JobManagers, configured them with the relevant savepoint and resource specs, and let them coordinate the TaskManagers. Each deploy walked through the full sequence of taking a savepoint, triggering the JM pods to tear down TM pods, tearing down the JM pods, and then starting the new FlinkDeployment’s JMs using the recently taken savepoint, which then brought up the new TM pods. For a real-time business like Lyft, this was unacceptable for several of our most important use cases.The fix for this was FlinkBlueGreenDeployments, a newer CRD that maintains underlying FlinkDeployment objects so a new version can come up alongside the old one before any cutover. This feature was still under development when we started testing it internally; we hit a bug in how the operator renamed Flink configuration fields under BlueGreen, and contributed a minor upstream fix. Benefiting from the open-source community’s efforts and being able to contribute back further reinforced our decision to move to an open-source solution.AutoscalingThe Apache operator’s autoscaler uses metrics like operator busyness, backpressure, and record backlog in Kafka and Kinesis to adjust each job’s parallelism. Traffic across most of Lyft’s use cases is highly variable and stream processing is expensive, so autoscaling was, in theory, an obvious win. In practice, our Flink version (v1.17) required apps to restart in order to rescale, and the apps that would benefit the most from autoscaling were precisely the ones that couldn’t afford restart-induced downtime.Upgrading to Flink v1.19 unlocked two important changes. First, it unlocked in-place autoscaling. Jobs could change parallelism without restarting, which both preserved data freshness and avoided the spiky catch-up traffic we used to see when jobs resumed from offsets that were a few minutes old. Second, it enabled an upgrade to the new Amazon Kinesis Source Connector, which emits record backlog metrics for Kinesis streams the same way the Kafka source does. This gave the autoscaler the signal it needed to make scaling decisions on Kinesis-bound jobs, which had previously been a blind spot.AutotuningAutotuning appealed to us for two main reasons. It promised dynamic right-sizing to cut cloud costs, and it spared our devs from tuning resource configurations by hand. However, we ran into an unexpected problem after we rolled this feature out.Our Apache Beam workloads run user code in a Python SDK harness, which lives outside the Flink memory model. The Apache operator didn’t register that we were reserving memory for those Python processes inside the JVM overhead allocation. We had been tucking it there for years because most of our jobs barely touched their JVM overhead anyway. This hack worked until we enabled autotuning. The operator saw that these memory pools were not really used by Flink, and reclaimed them, OOM-killing TaskManagers across our Beam fleet. We ultimately moved the Python harness out of the Flink container entirely, running it as a sidecar in the same pod with its own resource limits.Another awkward property of autotuning is that it doesn’t play well with in-place autoscaling. To tune a job’s resources, the operator has to restart it. We weren’t willing to give up either feature, so we settled on a two-tier approach where business-critical applications that power pricing, routing, and similar real-time decisions disable autotuning and keep in-place autoscaling. Less critical applications that could tolerate some downtime use both autotuning and autoscaling with restarts.KarpenterThese features also made our node infrastructure obsolete. Before autotuning, we bin-packed pods onto AWS nodes efficiently by enforcing 1:4 or 1:8 CPU:memory ratios with power-of-two values. Autotuning broke this. The same application could have very different ratios from one tuning cycle to the next, and a static node pool could not keep up. We adopted Karpenter, which provisions EC2 nodes on demand based on what each pod actually needs, optimizing for cost or utilization as appropriate.This two-tier autotuning model produced an additional unexpected efficiency win related to unused spend (the share of compute resources we are paying for that ends up unallocated). If we are paying for an 8-core node with 32GB of memory, but only allocate 4 cores and 16GB, half of the cost of the node is unused. We had already deployed a custom Kubernetes pod scheduler on our EKS cluster that uses a “most-allocated” strategy, packing pods onto busy nodes first. When autoscaling restarted apps to rescale them, the pods had a chance to move from under-allocated nodes to densely packed ones, letting us shed underutilized nodes.ConclusionThis migration was a multi-quarter journey that often felt like changing the engines on a plane mid-flight. It took longer than expected to completely sunset our in-house operator, as there was a mess of state-machine quirks, memory model mismatches, and CRDs that didn’t translate cleanly. However, the difference in the platform after completing this migration is hard to overstate; the operator maintenance that used to eat engineering time on every Flink upgrade has been minimized, and the autoscaler is doing what we had hoped, which is right-sizing a fleet that had been overprovisioned by a few million dollars per year.The important, but hard-to-quantify benefit is that we stopped being the only contributors to our operator and infrastructure. When we noticed the BlueGreen bug, we filed an issue and a fix landed upstream within days. Our team’s posture changed from “we maintain this thing” to “we use this thing, and sometimes improve it for everyone,” which is a much better place to be. What’s next is the work we actually wanted to focus on from the start. We’re building faster feedback loops for marketplace pricing, handling autonomous vehicle telemetry, and scaling streaming primitives for Lyft’s next chapter. The Apache operator finally gave us the breathing room to work on these challenging problems.AppreciationSpecial thanks to Anirudh Adkar and Ravi Magham, who provided guidance to us throughout the project, and Janice Lee, Rohan Varshney, and Yigal Kassel for their contributions to the team’s operations. The migration would not have been possible without their efforts.Finally, thanks to our many internal customers of Lyft’s Streaming Compute platform, who bore with us and provided ample helpful feedback throughout the migration, including but not limited to Kyle Bilton and Taylor Wilson.Lyft is hiring! If you love the idea of solving ambiguous problems in technology and infrastructure, visit Lyft Careers to see our openings.Rerouting the Stream: How Lyft Moved to the Apache Flink Kubernetes Operator was originally published in Lyft Engineering on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Evolving the cloud-native foundation for the next generation of AI
summary: Building a cloud-native foundation for AI The relationship between model innovation and AI infrastructure has never been more clear; as AI becomes more capable, the platform underneath it matters even more. Agents are fundamentally changing how applications work, and with that, what organizations need from the cloud. Learn how to build a cloud-native AI foundation Cloud-native practices gave organizations the scale, flexibility and resilience to build a generation of distributed applications. Agents build on that foundation, but they work differently, placing new demands on it. Unlike applications designed around more predictable workflows, agents behave in entirely new ways, gathering information and deep intelligence from across the business, using tools, making decisions, and coordinating work across long-running processes. To complete complex tasks, they pause for approval, respond to new information in real time and change course as conditions evolve. All this changes what the platform needs to deliver. Customers need infrastructure that adapts as demand changes, applications that remain reliable as work becomes more dynamic, and the visibility and control to understand what is happening across the system. Meeting those needs doesn’t mean starting over, but it does require that the cloud-native foundation organizations already rely on, to evolve. Compute, storage and networking need to work together. Application platforms need to make it easier to build and run AI workloads. Open technologies need to give customers flexibility without adding unnecessary complexity. The platform decisions organizations make today are increasingly strategic, shaping how effectively they can put AI to work for their business. Evolving the cloud-native foundation is essential to helping organizations get more from AI today while giving them the flexibility to take advantage of new capabilities as they emerge. Optimize infrastructure for AI workloads The true measure of AI infrastructure is the useful work it enables. AI workloads rarely place the same demands on infrastructure from beginning to end. Different parts of the work may need accelerated compute, CPUs, fast access to data or connectivity across applications and environments. The answer isn’t simply more capacity, but rather, to match the right resources to the right work at the right time. That makes coordination across the infrastructure extremely important. Compute, storage and networking need to work together as demands change. When they do, teams can spend less time managing infrastructure and more time focused on the applications and outcomes that matter to their business. Economics matter, too. Infrastructure needs to be tuned to the demands of the application and the business value it delivers, with the right balance of performance, reliability and cost across the complete workload. Basecamp Research is one example. The company used Azure to assemble 9.7 trillion nucleotides for EDEN, its therapeutic-design models, and reported laboratory validation across three therapeutic applications within about three weeks. In this example, AI didn’t simply require more infrastructure, it needed AI infrastructure that was coordinated and designed around the outcome – bringing together the compute, data and platform capabilities needed to move complex work forward. As Glen Gowers, co-founder of Basecamp Research put it: “To really be successful here, we need those three ingredients to come together. We need someone scaling the data; that’s us. But someone who really knows how to scale models and scale compute is Microsoft.” Leadership takeaway: Measure success by the useful work AI completes. Judge infrastructure investment by the performance, reliability and cost of delivering those outcomes, with compute, storage and networking operating as one system. Turn open-source innovation into production capability Open technologies have long helped drive cloud innovation, and AI is accelerating that pace. New models, frameworks and cloud-native technologies give organizations more choice in how they build and adapt applications. That opportunity builds on an established cloud-native foundation. Gartner forecasts that by 2028, 95% of new AI agent deployment will use Kubernetes.1 Reusing established components can shorten the path to production, allowing developers to focus on differentiated business capabilities rather than rebuilding the foundation. More choice can also bring more complexity. Taking advantage of open-source innovation often requires specialized expertise to integrate, manage and maintain technologies in production. That expertise is hard to find and even harder to scale. We need to make these capabilities accessible to more businesses, without requiring every organization to build and maintain that expertise themselves. Azure helps reduce that burden. Services like Azure Kubernetes Service give teams access to open-source innovation while helping manage the complexity and risk of running it in production. This makes it easier for more businesses to take advantage of open technologies while preserving the flexibility to adapt with changing needs. Leadership takeaway: Choose a platform that helps turn open-source freedom into business advantage. Preserve the ability to adapt and optimize while reducing the expertise and operating effort required to sustain those choices in production. Align AI infrastructure costs with business value As more organizations put AI into production, understanding the economics becomes increasingly important. AI investment starts with an expectation of business value: faster decisions, more responsive services or greater capacity to get useful work done. Then, it’s evaluating whether the value justifies the investment to deliver it. FinOps can help teams understand that return and make more informed decisions in this area. For customers, that starts with understanding the full investment required to run AI applications and how to optimize it as workloads scale. Models represent a significant expense, with token usage and agent behavior influencing spending. Compute, storage, networking and operations also factor into the equation. Considering these together helps customers make more informed decisions about where to optimize. Learn FinOps best practices for compute Teams can’t simply place their bets on spending less. They need to carefully consider that a more capable model or additional infrastructure that costs more may be the right choice if it produces greater value long-term. Teams need to understand the full cost, establish ownership and put guardrails in place as they scale. From there, they can use business outcomes to decide where to optimize and where to invest. Leadership takeaway: Manage AI investment against the business return it needs to deliver. Evaluate model and platform costs together, then use evidence of outcome value to decide where to optimize and where to invest. Transform cloud operations with agentic AI Operations teams are already stretched thin, keeping critical services running while balancing competing priorities and constant change. AI adds new complexity, and it also creates an opportunity to change how those environments are managed. Cloud-native operations gave teams a new model for managing infrastructure, bringing increased automation, visibility and resilience. Agentic operations build on that foundation, bringing deeper intelligence across applications and infrastructure by connecting signals from otherwise disconnected systems. This helps teams identify issues earlier and resolve them faster, while increasing automation and continuously improving how their environments perform; all within the tools they already use. Over time, AI can help operations teams move from reacting to problems toward anticipating and addressing them before they disrupt the business. As these capabilities mature, more actions can be automated within defined controls, with people remaining in the loop and accountable for critical decisions. When operations teams have greater reach without additional manual effort, reliability, performance and cost are continuously improved while critical services remain uninterrupted. Leadership takeaway: Invest in operations that can anticipate problems and coordinate action across the environment. Expand autonomy as capabilities are validated, with clear controls and human accountability protecting critical business services. Automate operations with Azure SRE Agent Build a cloud-native AI foundation on Azure Azure serves as the foundation customers need to put AI to work at scale. That means infrastructure designed around the complete workload, access to open innovation without unnecessary complexity, and a clear view of cost and business value. Greater intelligence across cloud operations helps teams anticipate issues and continuously improve how their environments perform as application needs evolve. We’re continuing to invest in capabilities across Azure that give customers greater flexibility in how they build and run AI applications. From secure, isolated environments for agents to simpler application deployment and the ability to run workloads across cloud and edge environments, these investments help customers take advantage of new capabilities without adding unnecessary operational complexity. Get started with Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) AI is changing what applications can do, and Azure has already evolved to support that shift. The cloud platform has to evolve with them. Years of focused engineering investment have built the foundation for some of the most advanced AI workloads running today, with continued innovation to support what comes next. Build for the next generation of AI Platform value compounds when improvements reinforce one another: faster information access keeps compute productive, operational insight exposes waste, and open technologies preserve room to adapt. The leadership task is to make those gains work together. That is the next chapter of cloud native: a foundation that turns advances in AI into dependable business value. title: [Engineering at Meta] How Meta Built Forum With AI-Native Engineering
summary: Meta’s newest app, Forum, is for anyone who wants to go deeper into the conversations in their Facebook groups. To build Forum, Meta engineers adopted a whole new way of working by bringing an AI agent into the development cycle. We’re sharing insights into what it took to build Forum with agentic AI: how we adapted the codebase, tested frameworks and internal tooling for agentic execution, what worked, and what didn’t. Forum is a standalone Groups app that a small team built from scratch. It’s also where we tested a different way of working: treating an AI agent as a participant in the engineering process rather than a faster way to type. That experiment needed a definition of success, and ours wasn’t code volume. We measured verified, production-ready outcomes — changes that build, pass tests, and survive review. From Human-In-The-Loop to Human-On-The-Loop Pointing AI at the coding step alone doesn’t change much. Our results compounded as we extended the approach to the stages around implementation — planning, building, testing, and verification. The clearest way to see the shift is in who owns each step. With human-in-the-loop, the engineer drives every step and the AI assists inside it by autocompleting a function, suggesting a fix, or answering a question. Each iteration advances at the pace of the person driving it. With human-on-the-loop, the agent runs the iteration itself — plan, implement, build, test, correct, repeat — while the engineer sets the goal, watches the run, steps in when it drifts, and approves the result. The person’s job moves from executing the steps to owning the outcome and holding the quality bar. This is the target we are driving toward, not a finished state: some stages run autonomously today, while others still keep an engineer in each iteration. When the engineer supervises, work stops being strictly sequential. Cycles that used to run one at a time can overlap, and an engineer’s time goes to direction and judgment rather than to sitting through the loop. But that only holds if what comes back can be trusted. Without verification, AI-generated code creates a familiar problem — plausible output that no one has confirmed actually works, which an engineer then has to read, debug, and often discard. Weak signals don’t remove the constraint; they move it from writing code to reviewing code that looks finished and isn’t. So we set the bar at verification rather than compilation. Compiling isn’t the finish line — a task is complete only once automated tests and visual checks have passed. Agents check their own work before an engineer sees it, which means what reaches review is a smaller set of higher-confidence results rather than a pile of output to sift through. Less gets generated, and less gets discarded. Every shipped outcome still carries an engineer’s sign-off; our effort went into making that sign-off fast and well-evidenced, with build results, test outcomes, and recorded verification sessions attached to the change. With the engineer outside of every cycle, the loop has to run safely on its own. Four capabilities make that possible: Planning as technical specification: Agentic execution requires extreme precision. Ambiguity that an engineer might resolve through intuition results in agent failure. We invested in rigorous upstream decomposition and machine-readable context, which tightened the engineering loop for engineers and agents alike. Automated verification inside the loop is the force multiplier: We integrated automated pass/fail signals — build status, unit tests, and UI spec matching — directly into the agent loop. This enabled asynchronous development producing ready-to-review pull requests with pre-populated test plans and recorded verification sessions. Verification is the hard part to get right, and how much we can safely hand to the loop is gated by how much we can trust the verifiers. Simulated user testing with agents: We deployed navigation agents that interact with the live app exactly like a person would. These agents perform actions, read the screen, and report regressions. Navigation agents are able to run the same verification paths continuously. Agentic production operations: After launch, agents help automate root-cause analysis. When someone using Forum submits feedback, the agents use that feedback to investigate possible regressions. The agents then forward the analysis to engineers who decide the next course of action. The Operating Model That ownership model needs machinery with five key components: Rules are permanent project instructions. When the agent repeats a mistake more than twice, we encode the correction once, for everyone. Skills turn team conventions into loadable steps the agent can invoke. Agents automate checks that previously required a manual pass. Commands chain skills and agents into workflows. They assess complexity, reproduce a bug, plan and implement a fix, create the pull request, and run a multi-stage review. Hooks are automated triggers, such as running a linter after every agent turn, checking simulator connectivity before install, and validating tests before a pull request is created. Adapting the Environment to the Models The biggest gains came from changing our code and tooling, not our prompts. Architectural legibility over inherited complexity: We worked to keep Forum’s codebase as straightforward as possible and chose to modularize key pieces of the architecture in order to get the benefits of battle-tested infrastructure while also letting the agents plug and play easily. Where we couldn’t easily do so, we rebuilt from scratch, trading reuse for agentic throughput, and it proved rewarding in development speed. Agents learn patterns from the code they read. Fix a weak pattern once and every future agent session inherits the improvement; leave it and the same shortcut shows up in everything the agent writes next. Give agents tools, not descriptions: Our main failure mode was the agent losing track of where it was in the app — editing the home feed when asked to change the group home screen, or guessing at screen coordinates. So instead of describing the app to the agent, we gave it tools to check: read the live view hierarchy from the simulator, list the elements actually on screen, and look up the path to a target view — all before it acts. Misdirected edits dropped sharply. We applied the same approach wherever agents touched our systems: give the agent a way to check state directly rather than a description to reason from. Build-level isolation for safe AI prototyping: As Forum matured toward production, we wanted early-stage prototypes and agent-generated experiments to have room to run while keeping the production app strictly limited to finished, reviewed work. We wanted a stronger guarantee than feature gating alone, where prototype code still exists inside the production build. Our solution was a separate build flavor, a sandbox app that shares the exact same codebase, frameworks, and design system as production, but compiles prototype code out of the production build entirely via a plugin/socket architecture. This gave us three things at once: Designers and cross-functional partners could prototype freely using AI tools without needing an engineer in the loop for each change. Anything built in the sandbox could be ported directly to production with no rebuild. No prototype code could crash the production app because it physically didn’t exist in that build. The pattern let us keep fast AI iteration after we had real people using the app to protect. Finding Real Bugs With AI Stress Testing Adapting the environment did more than make the agent faster to build with — it made the agent a tester. We didn’t point it at one specific defect. Instead, we set up repeatable stress scenarios that mimic real user behavior (aggressive scrolling, random group browsing, rapid navigation, repeated media loading) and ran them routinely across builds. Because these runs produce consistent signals (crashes, memory growth, page faults, UI regressions), the agent can triage anomalies, narrow to the triggering sequence, and then investigate the root cause. One such run surfaced a memory issue. The agent isolated a repro, proposed a fix, and verified it — all during development, before the app reached users. The fix materially reduced on-device memory growth and page faults across repeated stress sessions. While engineers made the architectural decisions, the detection and regression monitoring were automated and repeatable; once an anomaly was detected, the agent could reproduce → isolate → propose a fix → verify with the same harness. Applying the Same Discipline to Forum’s Feed We applied the human-on-the-loop approach in two places: Building the stack: Agents mapped the architectural options and trade-offs; engineers then evaluated and chose. What we deliberately kept human was the target — deciding what a good outcome looks like is a product judgment, not something the system should define for itself. Operating the stack: Questions that used to require whichever engineer knew the relevant code path now go to an investigation agent that gathers what it needs and posts a write-up with suggested fixes. After hand-scoring a batch of real investigations we arrived at a workflow where the agent compresses the mechanical work and delivers a structured write-up to an engineer, who then validates whether a finding is a real bug or an intentional trade-off. What improved quality wasn’t better prompting. It was context. One recurring category of investigation came back weak until we gave the agent the same pointers to the relevant code, example queries, and design docs that we’d give any new engineer on day one. The quality of that category jumped. The difference from human onboarding is that you train once, and every future session starts from it. Did It Work? Beyond shipping faster, we shipped cleaner. Continuous verification surfaced systemic issues — like the memory bottleneck above — during development rather than after launch. The results show up in the performance profile: Quality, found early: The autonomous stress-testing loop caught and fixed the aforementioned memory issue during development rather than post-launch, roughly halving memory use and page faults. Velocity: Forum reached core feature parity with Facebook Groups in eight weeks, with AI handling much of the routine implementation so engineers could focus on architecture, product decisions, and quality. Leverage that lasted: After launch, agent-driven investigation helped engineers triage and root-cause user feedback. The AI did more than generate code. It tightened our quality loop, helping a small team deliver a high-quality app with less ongoing rework. What Worked, and What Did Not Acknowledgements We thank Neeharika Sinha, Jane Kou, Gang Yang, Guohao Zhang, Zeya Zhang, Kinnary Jangla, andYonghui Lu for their valuable contributions. title: [Engineering at Meta] 2026 World Cup: Breaking Records, Spiky Charts and Reliability at Scale
summary: Every four years, the World Cup becomes the largest planned stress test of our infrastructure. This year it also set an all-time record! There are a few moments throughout the year, like New Years Eve, that really let us see the collective impact of everything we’ve built — but none are bigger than the quadrennial World Cup tournament. The 2026 World Cup broke records across messaging, video, recommendations, and networking at the same time. Some highlights: WhatsApp: More than 30 million messages per second during the July 19 final (Argentina vs. Spain), 1.23x the peak of New Year’s Eve 2026 and an all-time platform record. The previous record had already fallen 12 days earlier, during the Round of 16 match between Argentina and Egypt, at 29 million messages per second. Messenger, Threads, and Instagram Direct: 49 million messages per minute at peak. Instagram: Recommendation system traffic up to 80% higher week-over-week. Final-squad players collectively added +213.6 million activated followers — a 6.6% increase — with combined followings surging from 3.26 billion to 3.47 billion. Live video: Watch time spiked +90% on Instagram and +242% on Facebook, versus the July baseline. Threads: 1.5 billion impressions on tournament-tagged posts, reaching about 15 million people daily and peaking at 25 million on July 6. Facebook: 80 million posts mentioning the World Cup. Traffic Followed the Breaks, Not the Ball Every World Cup match caused surges in traffic. During the final, for example, traffic surged +46% in about four minutes at the end of regular time, and +57% in about 15 minutes at the final whistle. But by lining game events up against global egress traffic we discovered a striking pattern – surges in sharing were primarily happening during breaks (hydration breaks, halftime, extra time, the final whistle, the awards ceremony). The end-of-regulation whistle produced the single biggest peak of the tournament. It wasn’t the gameplay that moved our charts. It was the conversations after it. The world came to Meta to watch the game and to share what it made them feel. Every capacity decision below follows from that one pattern. Layered Systems, No Manual Intervention Those spikes were absorbed by systems built for exactly this. Taiji balanced load across datacenters, Katran and Proxygen handled L4/L7 traffic distribution, our global load balancing system routed users to the best-positioned edge, and AutoScaling provisioned capacity on demand. Region-Specific Capacity Months before kickoff, Meta’s edge teams analyzed network capacity and worked closely with ISP partners so that upgrades landed where they would most improve quality of experience for end users. That targeted pre-build is now permanent capacity that will keep serving demand long after the tournament. Instagram: Preparing for 39 Consecutive Days of Surges For Instagram, the tournament meant 39 straight days of traffic spikes as billions of fans checked scores, posted Stories, and flooded Feed during breaks. Machine learning inference, Feed serving, Stories, Explore, and data infrastructure all had to absorb it without degrading the experience. During the final, halftime Instagram Feed traffic rose 76% above the previous day in the minute the match ended, and stayed about 21% above for the following two hours. Our approach rested on four things, deployed incrementally as the tournament moved from group stage to final. Capacity buffers: Our products went into the tournament with sufficient capacity, which meant real buffers were available to allocate. We pre-provisioned significant additional capacity across all serving tiers so that spikes never had to wait on autoscaling to catch up. These dedicated buffers were our single most effective lever of the tournament. Country-level graceful degradation: For high-risk matches, we shed non-critical background load in the top-traffic nations (Brazil, Argentina, India, Indonesia, Spain) to protect core functionality. Cascade prevention: So spikes at the serving layer couldn’t propagate into downstream data systems. Early warning signals These alerted us before we approached capacity thresholds, rather than after. All of this, including the phased deployment timeline and the degradation activation criteria, is now a reusable runbook for future large-scale events like the 2028 Olympics. WhatsApp: 8.4 Billion Messages in Five Minutes Goals and the final whistle drove WhatsApp spikes lasting four to five minutes at a time. In its single highest-traffic five-minute window, WhatsApp delivered nearly 8.4 billion messages without interruption. That came from months of preparation. More than 100 internal services were load-tested and resized ahead of the tournament, then retested, revalidated, and resized as the bracket narrowed and demand climbed. Two things we’d normally do, we didn’t. We didn’t shift load between regions. For past high-traffic events, our default has been to spread demand across multiple regions, letting capacity in quieter parts of the world absorb the spike. That works when peaks land hours apart — a global New Year’s Eve, for example. This event was different. Every region peaked in the same instant, so there was no idle capacity to borrow. Instead of deriving regional demand from a global multiplier, we forecast each region’s peak on its own terms. We didn’t freeze. The other standard playbook move for a major event is to pause continuous deployment and hold off on riskier operations like disaster recovery exercises. This time we skipped the freeze entirely, on the strength of years of reliability enhancement. Teams shipped on their normal cadence throughout the entire event window, including during the peak moment itself. We Stay Ready Year-Round Enabling connection in moments like this doesn’t just happen. Powering every message sent, every follower, and every Reel shared in real time across 48 teams and 104 matches is a story of infrastructure and product working as one. Capacity planning, load testing, traffic management, and rapid incident response come together across these teams so that billions of people can connect in the moments that matter most — like an entire continent celebrating a last-minute goal at the same second. title: [Kubernetes] The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know
summary:
In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode. Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25. Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features. Deprecation of cgroup v1Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1. Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true, so the kubelet does not start on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration file, but removal will follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy. Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support. If you are still on a release older than v1.35, migrate every Linux node to cgroup v2 before upgrading, or plan to set the temporary failCgroupV1: false override. If you are already on v1.35 or later, confirm that every Linux node runs cgroup v2 (or that you intentionally keep the override). Under the default configuration, a remaining cgroup v1 node fails during kubelet startup. For kubeadm-managed clusters, Kubernetes v1.35 also makes this an earlier, stricter check. The SystemVerification preflight check, provided by k8s.io/system-validators, returns an error during kubeadm init, kubeadm join, and kubeadm upgrade when it detects cgroup v1 with kubelet v1.35 or later; with an older kubelet, the check remains a warning. See kubernetes/system-validators#1.12.1 release notes for details. The top FAQs cover three main areas: why to migrate, the benefits and drawbacks, and key points to keep in mind when using cgroup v2. Limitations of cgroup v1 and Improvements with cgroup v2The Linux kernel documentation describes both interfaces: cgroup v1 documentation cgroup v2 documentation Let's enumerate some known issues. active_file memory is not considered available memoryThe kubelet treats active_file memory as not reclaimable. For I/O-intensive workloads, a large page cache can therefore make the kubelet report memory pressure and evict Pods. This is a known kubelet issue (kubernetes/kubernetes#43916); migrating to cgroup v2 does not by itself change that calculation. The documented workaround is to set equal memory requests and limits for containers that perform intensive I/O, after measuring an appropriate value. Memory QoS updates in Kubernetes v1.36Memory QoS was introduced as an alpha feature in Kubernetes v1.22 and updated in v1.27. It remains alpha in v1.36, but now separates memory throttling from memory reservation and adds tiered memory protection: Memory QoS is available only on Linux nodes that use cgroup v2. It relies on the cgroup v2 memory controller: memory.high provides throttling, while memory.min and memory.low provide hard and soft protection when tiered reservation is enabled. cgroup v1 cannot provide this protection model. Enabling the MemoryQoS feature gate applies memory.high throttling to Burstable containers. The threshold is derived from the request, limit, and memoryThrottlingFactor (default 0.9). memoryReservationPolicy: None is the default. It does not write memory.min or memory.low. memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation maps Guaranteed Pod memory requests to memory.min (hard protection) and Burstable Pod requests to memory.low (soft protection). BestEffort Pods receive neither protection. The kubelet exposes Alpha metrics for the total memory.min and memory.low reservations on a node. Kernel 5.9 or later is recommended. On older kernels, memory.high reclaim can trigger a known livelock; from v1.36 the kubelet logs a warning when Memory QoS is enabled on an affected kernel. For example, to opt in to tiered protection: apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: KubeletConfiguration featureGates: MemoryQoS: true memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation memoryThrottlingFactor: 0.9 The overall Kubernetes recommendation is not to enable Alpha features in production; however, if you judge that memory QoS with tiered reservations is useful for your platform in production, make sure to test the configuration and account for hard-reserved memory before you enable the TieredReservation feature gate. See the Pod QoS documentation for the current mapping of Kubernetes QoS classes to cgroup v2 controls. Container-aware OOM handlingOn cgroup v2 nodes, the kubelet defaults singleProcessOOMKill to false. It therefore sets memory.oom.group for each container cgroup so that an OOM event kills all processes in that container together, rather than leaving a partially functioning multi-process container. Set singleProcessOOMKill: true only if you need the cgroup v1-compatible behavior where the kernel may kill one process at a time. See the KubeletConfiguration reference for this setting. This behavior is scoped to a container cgroup, not the whole Pod. Also, cgroup.kill is a separate administrative interface: writing 1 to it sends SIGKILL to every process in that cgroup and its descendants; it does not configure OOM behavior. The cgroup v2 memory controller additionally provides memory.events counters that monitoring systems and userspace OOM managers can observe. Rootless supportIn cgroup v1, delegating controllers to less privileged containers may be dangerous. Unlike cgroup v1, cgroup v2 officially supports delegation. Most implementations of rootless containers rely on systemd for delegating v2 controllers to non-root users. This delegation mechanism is separate from Kubernetes Pod user namespaces, which map container users to unprivileged host users. Pod user namespace support graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.36; check its filesystem, kernel, CRI runtime, and OCI runtime prerequisites before enabling it. What else? eBPF stories: In cgroup v1, device access controls are exposed through interface files. The cgroup v2 device controller has no interface files, and is implemented on top of cgroup BPF. Cilium attaches BPF cgroup programs for socket-based load balancing. Its default cgroup root is /run/cilium/cgroupv2. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) reports CPU, memory, and I/O contention at node, Pod, and container level. On supported clusters, the kubelet exposes PSI by default (KubeletPSI is stable and locked on). PSI requires cgroup v2, Linux 4.20 or later, CONFIG_PSI=y, and a kernel not booted with psi=0. The kubelet surfaces the data through the Summary API and /metrics/cadvisor. When migrating, update software that reads the cgroup filesystem directly. The migration guidance recommends cAdvisor v0.43.0 or later and lists compatible Java, Node.js, and automaxprocs versions. CPU weight conversion in newer OCI runtimescgroup v1 uses cpu.shares, whereas cgroup v2 uses cpu.weight. Newer OCI runtimes use an improved non-linear conversion that preserves the default priority and gives small CPU requests more usable granularity. The change is implemented in the OCI runtime rather than Kubernetes: it is available in crun v1.23 and runc v1.3.2. After upgrading a runtime, monitoring or policy tools that predict exact cpu.weight values may need updates. Read New Conversion from cgroup v1 CPU Shares to v2 CPU Weight for the formula, examples, and compatibility considerations. In-place resource updatesIn-place Pod vertical scaling graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.35. Kubernetes v1.36 then  (/blog/2026/04/30/kubernetes-v1-36-inplace-pod-level-resources-beta/) in-place vertical scaling for Pod-level resources by default, as a Beta feature. The kubelet coordinates changes between the Pod-level and container cgroups so that increases create headroom before container limits grow, while decreases constrain containers before shrinking the Pod-level boundary. Accurate aggregate enforcement for this v1.36 feature requires cgroup v2. Adopting cgroup version 2RequirementsHere's what you need to use cgroup v2 with Kubernetes. First up, you need to be using a version of Kubernetes with support for v2 cgroup management; that's been stable since Kubernetes v1.25 and all supported Kubernetes releases include this support. You need at least one Linux node; cgroup is a Linux-only concept Your OS install must run with cgroup v2 enabled The kernel version must be 5.8 or later (5.9 or later is recommended when using memory QoS) The container runtime must support cgroup v2. For example: containerd v1.4 or later supports cgroup v2; use containerd v2.0 or later for automatic cgroup-driver discovery CRI-O v1.20 or later The kubelet and the container runtime must both be configured to use the correct cgroup driver. See Configure the kubelet's cgroup driver to match the container runtime cgroup driver. For now, you can opt back in to use cgroup v1; the Kubernetes project recommends using cgroup v2, but in Kubernetes 1.36 (the current release) the cgroup v1 option remains supported as a fallback. That fallback is scheduled for removal in Kubernetes v1.38. If you are running an older cluster, plan to migrate; if you are setting up a new cluster with Linux nodes, you should prefer cgroup v2. In either case, review both the Kubernetes runtime documentation and (if relevant) the containerd compatibility matrix. kernel updates around cgroup v2When Kubernetes was first announced, in 2014, only v1 cgroup existed. Version 2 cgroup management first appeared in Linux kernel 4.5, released in 2016. In Linux 4.5, the cgroup v2 io, memory, and pids controllers were supported. Linux 4.15 added support for the cgroup v2 cpu controller. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) support began with Linux 4.20. The Kubernetes project does not recommend using cgroup v2 with a Linux kernel older than 5.2 due to lack of cgroup-level task freezer support. Kubernetes documents 5.8 as the minimum kernel version for cgroup v2; the root cgroup's system-level cpu.stat file was added in Linux 5.8. The memory.high livelock fix used by Memory QoS is present in Linux 5.9 and later. memory.peak was added in Linux 5.19. cgroup driver configurationConfigure the kubelet's cgroup driver to match the container runtime cgroup driver. If you use kubeadm to manage your cluster, Kubernetes recommends that you use the systemd cgroup driver, because kubeadm manages the kubelet as a systemd service. For other management tooling, check the documentation for the tool you're using to manage your cluster. If you can pick either option, I recommend using the systemd driver. Whatever tooling you've chosen, the kubelet automatically tries to detect the runtime's recommended cgroup driver. This automatic detection relies on using a runtime that implements the RuntimeConfig CRI RPC (for example: containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). If you're using a container runtime that supports cgroup v2 but doesn't support automatic cgroup driver detection, you can manually configure an override by editing the kubelet configuration file. For example: apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: KubeletConfiguration cgroupDriver: systemd Automatic discovery of the runtime's cgroup driver through the CRI, tracked by KEP-4033, graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.34. It requires a runtime that implements the RuntimeConfig CRI RPC (containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). When available, the kubelet uses the value reported by the runtime instead of its configured cgroupDriver value. Tools and commands for troubleshootingTools and commands that you should know about cgroups: stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup/: Check whether cgroup v2 is enabled; it returns cgroup2fs. systemctl list-units 'kube*' --type=slice or --type=scope: List Kubernetes-related units that systemd currently has in memory. bpftool cgroup list /sys/fs/cgroup/*: List all programs attached to the cgroup CGROUP. systemd-cgls /sys/fs/cgroup/*: Recursively show control group contents. systemd-cgtop: Show top control groups by their resource usage. tree -L 2 -d /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice: Show Pods' related cgroups directories. How to check if a Pod CPU or memory limit is successfully applied to the cgroup file?Work from the API object down to the node. Identify the node, then compare desired resources in the spec with the enacted values in status (in-place resize can leave those out of sync): kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}{"
"}' kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{range .spec.containers}{.name}{" spec	"}{.resources}{"
"}{end}' kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{range .status.containerStatuses}{.name}{" status	"}{.resources}{"
"}{end}' On that node, as root, with the systemd cgroup driver and cgroup v2 (these snippets also need jq). Pin the container with kubelet labels; a container name alone is not unique on a node. Use crictl ps -a if the container is not running: CONTAINER_ID=$(crictl ps \ --label io.kubernetes.pod.namespace=<namespace> \ --label io.kubernetes.pod.name=<pod-name> \ --name <container-name> -q | head -n1) # OCI view (not the CRI protobuf field names) crictl inspect "$CONTAINER_ID" | jq '.info.runtimeSpec.linux.resources' # Kernel cgroup path for this container PID=$(crictl inspect "$CONTAINER_ID" | jq -r '.info.pid') CGROUP="/sys/fs/cgroup$(awk -F: '$1=="0"{print $3}' /proc/$PID/cgroup)" cat "$CGROUP/cpu.weight" # request.cpu → shares → weight; not a limit cat "$CGROUP/cpu.max" # limit.cpu as "quota period"; unlimited is "max <period>" cat "$CGROUP/memory.max" # limit.memory; unlimited is "max" # Pod-level cgroup (parent slice), used by Pod-level resources cat "$(dirname "$CGROUP")/cpu.max" "$(dirname "$CGROUP")/memory.max" # Present when MemoryQoS is enabled cat "$CGROUP/memory.high" "$CGROUP/memory.min" "$CGROUP/memory.low" SCOPE=$(basename "$CGROUP") systemctl show "$SCOPE" \ -p CPUWeight -p CPUQuotaPerSecUSec -p CPUQuotaPeriodUSec -p MemoryMax Do not treat info.runtimeSpec.linux.cgroupsPath as a filesystem path when the runtime uses the systemd driver; that value is a systemd unit path (slice:runtime:id), not a directory under /sys/fs/cgroup. Expected mapping at each layer: Kubernetes: spec.containers.resources (desired) and status.containerStatuses.resources (enacted after in-place resize). Pod-level resources are on spec.resources and the parent pod slice. CRI (kubelet → runtime; these protobuf names stay cgroup v1-style even on v2): cpu_shares, cpu_quota, cpu_period, memory_limit_in_bytes, plus unified for Memory QoS. crictl inspect does not show these names; it shows the OCI spec the runtime derived from them. OCI spec: linux.resources.cpu.{shares,quota,period}, linux.resources.memory.limit, and linux.resources.unified. The runtime converts shares, quota, and period into cgroup v2 files. After upgrading crun or runc, the shares-to-weight formula may change; see CPU weight conversion. systemd scope: CPUWeight, CPUQuotaPerSecUSec, CPUQuotaPeriodUSec, MemoryMax. Unlimited or unset values often appear as  or infinity. cgroupfs: cpu.weight (from CPU request; an unset request still yields the default of 2 shares), cpu.max, and memory.max on the container scope. Memory QoS adds memory.high, memory.min, and memory.low. Further reading Kubernetes 1.31: Moving cgroup v1 Support into Maintenance Mode Kubernetes v1.36: Tiered Memory Protection with Memory QoS Kubernetes v1.36: PSI Metrics for Kubernetes Graduates to GA Kubernetes 1.25: cgroup v2 graduates to GA KubeCon NA 2022 cgroup v2: Before You Jump In by Tony Gosselin & Mike Tougeron, Adobe Systems KubeCon NA 2022 Cgroupv2 Is Coming Soon To a Cluster Near You - David Porter, Google & Mrunal Patel, RedHat KubeCon EU 2020 Kubernetes On cgroup v2 by Giuseppe Scrivano, Red Hat. This blog only covers the basic requirements and configuration of Kubernetes components. It will not include how to enable cgroup fs in OS distributions. For migration, you can refer to migrating cgroup v2

title: [CNCF] Filtering and reducing AI agent telemetry with the OpenTelemetry Collector
summary: Turn on an AI coding agent’s telemetry and it throws a wall of text at you. It’s expensive to store and what’s worse, you can’t make sense of it. It’s all OpenTelemetry native, though. So you can shape it in the Collector before sending it to a telemetry backend. Which leaves one question. What do you actually need? The requirement isn’t to collect less, it’s to keep what answers questions I gave Claude Code a small task. Fix two failing tests, add a few boundary tests. It did. With every content flag on, that one run produced 181 telemetry records and 289 KB of JSON. What I needed was answers to these six questions: QuestionWhat answers itWhat is this costing, per model?claude_code.cost.usageTokens per session, and how much is cache?claude_code.token.usage by typeWhich tools fail, and how often?tool_result events, successAre people rejecting the agent’s edits?tool_decision eventsWhere is the latency?llm_request spans, ttft_msWhat broke?api_error events, error_class Every answer is a counter or a short attribute. I don’t need prompts, file bodies or diffs. If no dashboard, alert, or query reads a field, it isn’t observability. It’s storage you’re paying to index. Where the volume actually lives An agent runs a loop: Prompt, model call, tool call, result, decide, repeat. One interaction is a claude_code.interaction span with an llm_request child per model turn and a tool child per tool call. With OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT on, each tool span gets a tool.output event holding whatever the tool returned. That’s a directory listing. When the tool is Read, the event is the file. A 40 KB file becomes a 40 KB span event. Logs have the same shape. tool_result and tool_decision events carry tool_parameters, the full arguments to the tool. For a Write that’s the whole file. Same content as the span event, stored twice. Metrics carry identity instead. Every data point has session.id, user.id, user.email and two account ids. Each new session created a fresh set of time series that never goes away. Twenty five sessions gave me 300 series for eight metrics. The default instrumentation is written for debugging one agent run, not for running a fleet. Tool content lands in traces and logs both. Metrics are keyed on attributes that belong on the resource, or nowhere. None of that is wrong for a single developer watching a single session. It’s wrong at 200 sessions a day. The agent won’t change its defaults for you, so the pipeline has to. What we’re building One OTLP receiver that’ll ingest Claude Code’s internal telemetry. Every signal is fanned into two pipelines, a raw one and an optimized one, each with its own exporter, all six landing in the same Grafana LGTM container. The raw pipeline is the control group. It carries a service.name and a batch processor. Nothing else. The optimized pipeline carries the processors we’ll add in this tutorial. The same receiver feeds both, so both paths see byte identical input. That’s what makes the comparison honest. Both data sets land in Grafana. One dashboard reads both and draws them side by side, red for raw, green for optimized. Cardinality, bytes per minute, record counts. The gap between the lines is the storage you stop paying for. In production you’d point the raw exporters at object storage, or drop them altogether. Here they point at Grafana because I want to show you the difference. # docker-compose.yaml services: lgtm: image: grafana/otel-lgtm:0.33.1 ports: - "3000:3000" collector: image: otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.161.0 depends_on:  volumes: - ./config.yaml:/etc/otelcol-contrib/config.yaml:ro ports: - "4317:4317" - "4318:4318" receivers: otlp: protocols: grpc: endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317 http: endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318 exporters: otlp/lgtm_raw_logs: endpoint: lgtm:4317 tls: insecure: true sending_queue: enabled: true otlp/lgtm_opt_logs: endpoint: lgtm:4317 tls: insecure: true sending_queue: enabled: true # four more exactly like this: # otlp/lgtm_raw_metrics, otlp/lgtm_raw_traces, # otlp/lgtm_opt_metrics, otlp/lgtm_opt_traces service: pipelines: logs/raw: receivers:  processors:  exporters:  logs/optimized: receivers:  processors:  # the reduction goes here exporters:  # four more exactly like this: # metrics/raw, metrics/optimized, traces/raw, traces/optimized export CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 export CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1 export OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=otlp export OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp export OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4317 export OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1 export OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES=1 export OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 export OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1 Step 2. Logs: Drop, delete, trim, hash Filter. api_request carries a model name and a request id. Everything else on it lives in other signals. Drop the whole event. Roughly a quarter of log records. processors: filter/drop_api_request: error_mode: ignore logs: log_record: - 'attributes == "api_request"' Delete. Six attributes off every record. tool_parameters is the big one. prompt_length and response_length stay, so you still see size trends without the text. transform/logs_delete_fields: error_mode: ignore log_statements: - context: log statements: - delete_key(log.attributes, "prompt") - delete_key(log.attributes, "response") - delete_key(log.attributes, "tool_parameters") - delete_key(log.attributes, "workspace.host_paths") - delete_key(log.attributes, "user.email") - delete_key(log.attributes, "terminal.type") Hash and trim. Hash session.id and user.id, cap error at 256 characters. transform/logs_hash_and_trim: error_mode: ignore log_statements: - context: log statements: - set(log.attributes, Substring(SHA256(log.attributes), 0, 16)) where log.attributes != nil - set(log.attributes, Substring(SHA256(log.attributes), 0, 16)) where log.attributes != nil - set(log.attributes, Substring(log.attributes, 0, 256)) where log.attributes != nil and Len(log.attributes) > 256 Truncate the digest. A full SHA256 is 64 characters replacing a 36 character UUID, twice per record. The first time I ran this, log bytes went up. Sixteen hex characters is plenty. logs/optimized: receivers:  processors:  exporters:  Log bytes roughly halve. Step 3. Metrics: Delete the dimension The problem here is cardinality, not bytes. Delete six attributes from every data point and 300 series become 12 regardless if the content flags are on or off. transform/metrics_delete_fields: error_mode: ignore metric_statements: - context: datapoint statements: - delete_key(datapoint.attributes, "session.id") - delete_key(datapoint.attributes, "user.account_uuid") - delete_key(datapoint.attributes, "user.account_id") - delete_key(datapoint.attributes, "user.id") - delete_key(datapoint.attributes, "user.email") - delete_key(datapoint.attributes, "terminal.type") Sum the sessions, then convert. Claude Code exports delta temporality and Prometheus wants cumulative, so delta_to_cumulative has to sit at the end of this pipeline. With session.id gone, every running session writes into the same twelve series, and the converter only accepts points in timestamp order. Sum the sessions per window first. # 1. Collect two seconds of exports. The size is out of reach on purpose, # so the timeout is always what flushes. batch/metrics_window: send_batch_size: 1000000 send_batch_max_size: 0 timeout: 2s # 2. Put every metric of the same name under one resource. groupbyattrs/compact: {} # 3. Give every point in the window the same timestamp, then sum the points # whose attributes are now identical. transform/metrics_merge_sessions: error_mode: ignore metric_statements: - context: datapoint statements: - set(datapoint.time, TruncateTime(Now(), Duration("1s"))) - set(datapoint.start_time, datapoint.time) - context: metric statements: - aggregate_on_attributes("sum") # 4. Only now convert. On the raw pipeline too, or the raw side never # reaches Prometheus and there is nothing to compare against. delta_to_cumulative: max_stale: 5m metrics/optimized: receivers:  processors:  exporters:  Batch and wait two seconds, give everything one timestamp, add up the points, then convert. Optimized totals match raw to within half a percent. Note: This only works if one Collector sees every session, so behind a load balancer it belongs on a single gateway. Metric bytes fall by more than any other signal. Six attributes on every point was most of the payload. And, removing the session.id keeps the cardinality in check. Step 4. Traces: Trim, don’t sample Traces are the biggest stream and the one people want to sample first. I’ll use one filter and two transforms instead. Filter. Drop tool.execution when the tool succeeded. The parent span already has tool_name, duration_ms and result_tokens. The child is only valuable when it fails. This alone removes a fifth of the trace bytes. filter/drop_successful_tool_execution: error_mode: ignore traces: span: - 'name == "claude_code.tool.execution" and attributes == true and attributes == nil' Span context. Delete what repeats, hash what identifies. transform/traces_span: error_mode: ignore trace_statements: - context: span statements: - delete_key(span.attributes, "user_prompt") where span.name == "claude_code.interaction" - delete_key(span.attributes, "user.email") - delete_key(span.attributes, "terminal.type") - delete_key(span.attributes, "user.account_uuid") - delete_key(span.attributes, "user.account_id") - delete_key(span.attributes, "organization.id") - delete_key(span.attributes, "span.type") - delete_key(span.attributes, "tool_use_id") - delete_key(span.attributes, "request_id") - delete_key(span.attributes, "model") - delete_key(span.attributes, "stop_reason") - delete_key(span.attributes, "full_command") where span.attributes != nil and IsMatch(span.attributes, "(sk-ant-|gh_|AKIA{16}|(?i)(password|secret|token)\\s*=)") - set(span.attributes, Substring(SHA256(span.attributes), 0, 16)) where span.attributes != nil - set(span.attributes, Substring(SHA256(span.attributes), 0, 16)) where span.attributes != nil Twelve deletes. tool_use_id, request_id, model and stop_reason each have a twin in gen_ai.tool.call.id, gen_ai.response.id, gen_ai.request.model and gen_ai.response.finish_reasons. Keep the gen_ai.* semconv names. A dashboard that has never heard of Claude Code still understands those. The full_command statement is the one secret guard, on the one field that can carry a secret. Span event context. Cap content, output and diff at 512 characters, move them onto the span, and add content_truncated_by_pipeline so nobody mistakes a cut body for a short one. transform/traces_spanevent: error_mode: ignore trace_statements: - context: spanevent statements: - set(span.attributes, true) where spanevent.attributes != nil and Len(spanevent.attributes) > 512 - set(span.attributes, Substring(spanevent.attributes, 0, 512)) where spanevent.attributes != nil and Len(spanevent.attributes) > 512 - delete_key(spanevent.attributes, "content") # the same three statements for "output" and for "diff" Every span survives. The ls -la stays readable. A 40 KB file read does not, and that’s the point. traces/optimized: receivers:  processors:  exporters:  Trace bytes roughly halve without sampling. Sampling would cut further. I left it out because it trades away the one thing traces are for, pulling up the specific run someone is asking about. Agent interactions also run for minutes, and tail_sampling decides after decision_wait, so a tool that fails at minute three arrives after the verdict. If truncation isn’t enough, this is the next step. This block below keeps errors, slow traces, and 10 percent of the rest. tail_sampling: decision_wait: 120s num_traces: 50000 decision_cache: sampled_cache_size: 100000 non_sampled_cache_size: 100000 policies: - name: errors type: status_code status_code: status_codes:  - name: slow type: latency latency: threshold_ms: 60000 - name: baseline type: probabilistic probabilistic: sampling_percentage: 10 Step 5. Prove nothing you needed was lost The objection is always the same. “We lose data.” Let’s check. The Collector counts its own bytes. Turn on detailed self telemetry and send it to the same Grafana. service: telemetry: metrics: level: detailed readers: - periodic: interval: 10000 exporter: otlp: protocol: grpc endpoint: http://lgtm:4317 insecure: true Name the two paths and tag the metric points so the queries can tell them apart. Four processor definitions, then every pipeline picks up the ones it needs. resource/name_raw: attributes: - {key: service.name, value: claude-code-raw, action: upsert} resource/name_optimized: attributes: - {key: service.name, value: claude-code-optimized, action: upsert} transform/tag_raw: error_mode: ignore metric_statements: - context: datapoint statements: - set(datapoint.attributes, "raw") transform/tag_optimized: error_mode: ignore metric_statements: - context: datapoint statements: - set(datapoint.attributes, "optimized") service: pipelines: logs/raw: receivers:  processors:  exporters:  logs/optimized: receivers:  processors:  exporters:  metrics/raw: receivers:  processors:  exporters:  metrics/optimized: receivers:  processors:  exporters:  traces/raw: receivers:  processors:  exporters:  traces/optimized: receivers:  processors:  exporters:  The dashboard is three query shapes. # cardinality, from the data itselfcount by (pipeline) ({__name__=~”claude_code_.*”, pipeline=~”raw|optimized”})# bytes per minute, per signal, before and aftersum(increase(otelcol_exporter_enqueue_size_bytes_sum{exporter=”otlp/lgtm_raw_logs”}))sum(increase(otelcol_exporter_enqueue_size_bytes_sum{exporter=”otlp/lgtm_opt_logs”}))# record counts, per exportersum by (exporter) (otelcol_exporter_sent_log_records_total) otelcol_exporter_enqueue_size_bytes only exists at level: detailed with sending_queue enabled, and it’s labelled by exporter, not signal. Top row, cardinality. 300 raw, 12 optimized. In a real fleet the red line climbs with every session. Green is flat because there’s no per session dimension left to grow along. Middle row, bytes per minute per signal. The gap is what you stop paying for. Bottom row, record counts. Logs lose api_request, traces lose successful tool.execution, metrics arrive pre-summed. None of it is sampling. The second dashboard reads only the optimized stream and asks the six questions. Tokens by type, cost by model, log volume, lines added and removed. Twelve series, every panel populated, and all my questions answered. What’s next? If you’ve written off agent telemetry as “all prompts, nothing to dashboard,” the constraint is narrower than it looks. You don’t need the transcript in your backend. You need six answers. Use the layout above to configure processing and start cutting storage costs right away.

title: [Cloudflare] Localizing compliance at scale: achieving South Korea’s ISMS certification
summary: For ten days, auditors appointed by the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) sat together with us and worked through 80 controls. That is what it took for a company headquartered in the United States, operating a global network serving Korean users, to be certified in South Korea. Cloudflare has now obtained South Korea's Information Security Management System (ISMS) certification under the ISMS-P framework.For customers in Korea, this is more than a compliance checkbox. It is evidence that Cloudflare's security and privacy program has been examined not only for whether our controls exist, but for how they operate in the context of Korean law, the Korean language, and the particular expectations of Korean regulators.What a Korean user sees when they sign upThe most visible result of this work is the Cloudflare account sign-up page. In most parts of the world, the line that sits above the sign-up button reads: "By continuing, I agree to Cloudflare's terms, privacy policy, and cookie policy."A user signing up from South Korea sees something different. The Korean experience is triggered by the country selected at sign-up and by IP geolocation from within South Korea, and it breaks the same agreement into four separately labeled items, each marked required or optional, each linking to its full text, with an option to agree to all of them at once:모두 동의 (Agree to all) 서비스 약관 ( Terms of Service) 개인정보 수집 및 이용 ( Collection and use of personal information) 제한된 범위의 개인정보 해외 이전 ( Transfer of a limited amount of personal information overseas) 제한된 범위의 개인정보 제3자 제공 ( Sharing a limited amount of personal information with marketing third parties)The three required items are hard gates. The sign-up button stays disabled until all three are checked, so there is no path through the form that creates an account without an affirmative action on each one. The optional item governs marketing permission only, and leaving it unchecked has no effect on the account creation (it merely opts the user out of receiving marketing communications).The hard part: sign-up paths that never show a formItemizing consent on a form we control is straightforward. The difficulty was the sign-up paths that skip that form entirely.Globally, you can create a Cloudflare account with Google, Apple, or GitHub. Those flows hand the user to an identity provider and return with an authenticated identity, and they never render our own sign-up form, which is precisely where the four consent items live. There is no step in that handoff where we can present three required items, link each to its full Korean text, and require an affirmative action on each before the account exists. The identity provider's screen is not ours to change.We could either build a separate post-authentication consent gate for one country, or remove the paths that bypass the gate we already had. We chose the second. Social sign-up is not offered in South Korea, so every account created there goes through Cloudflare’s sign-up form, which enforces the required consents.The country signal is the same one available to any Cloudflare customer. Cloudflare derives a two-letter country code from the client IP address and exposes it on the request, as the CF-IPCountry header at the origin and as request.cf.country inside a Worker.
