Reduced to its essentials, the branch is a string comparison:// Illustrative: the shape of the check, not Cloudflare's own dashboard code. export default { async fetch(request) { // Two-letter country code derived from the client IP. // Same value as the CF-IPCountry request header. // Cloudflare's network populates this on the incoming request, so there is // no geolocation database, lookup service, or extra round trip of our own. const country = request.cf?.country; if (country === "KR") { return renderSignUp({ locale: "ko-KR", consent: "itemized", // four separate items, three of them required socialLogin: false, // no path that skips the consent form }); } return renderSignUp({ locale: "en-US", consent: "combined", socialLogin: true }); }, };What that does not show is why the country code is not the whole trigger. We document the limits of IP geolocation: it is an estimate rather than an exact science, addresses rotate and change ownership, and it should not be the only signal where the use case is critical to meeting the objectives of a local requirement. A Korean resident traveling abroad, or behind a VPN or a mobile carrier's NAT, may not arrive with a Korean address. So IP-based geolocation decides which form appears by default, but the country a user selects at sign-up overrides that and carries the decision from there. The IP address tells us where a request came from; only the user can tell us where they reside. Keeping those two apart is what makes the consent meaningful rather than presumed.It is a small feature. It took a country-level product decision, and a change to the account creation path.What ISMS is and why it mattersISMS is a detailed, localized certification standard. It covers security policy, access control, authentication and permission management, encryption, incident response, risk management, and disaster recovery, all assessed against how personal data actually moves through an organization's systems, and against Korea's Personal Information Protection Act and its associated regulatory guidelines.Certification requires an independent audit by an auditor appointed by KISA, a governmental institution affiliated with the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT), followed by review from a special committee. It is valid for three years, with an annual audit required to maintain it.The ISMS certification is primarily established under Article 47 of Korea's Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc., with the certification criteria and procedure set out in its Enforcement Decree and in the public notification on ISMS certification issued by MSIT.What the audit examinedCloudflare is already certified against ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27701, ISO/IEC 27017, ISO/IEC 27018 and many other globally recognized frameworks. ISMS does not replace any of them. It is a localization of the same principles, layered with Korean regulatory requirements, and that changes what auditors look for and how they look for it.The controls in scope started with the review of data flows. We presented detailed data flow diagrams showing every path by which employees could access personal information that Cloudflare collects, processes, and stores. The flows themselves are not Korea-specific. What was different was the form the evidence had to take: the auditors were not willing to work from a narrative description of how data moves, they wanted diagrams they could read and interrogate. For each one, they examined every access control layer and tested its effectiveness, across our internal systems, our public-facing websites, event pages, and the Cloudflare dashboard, covering the full lifecycle of a user's data from first interaction through to destruction. Those diagrams are not published here due to confidentiality.The audit also scrutinized the language and terminology of our consent collection: the exact wording at sign-up, the structure of each notification, and whether the items were presented separately and clearly. That is the kind of detail the ISMS framework is designed to surface.Why the timeline ran to a year and a halfPart of the answer is how audit cycles work. An ISMS audit covers a single annual period, and all evidence, documentation, and systems must reflect that period. Our preparation ran past one audit year and into the next, which meant retranslating updated policies for the new audit year, re-collecting and reassessing evidence, republishing an updated privacy policy, and absorbing formatting and design changes our marketing and website teams had introduced in the meantime.What the certificate coversKISA defines the certified scope as a service boundary rather than as an enumerated list of in-scope products. The Statement of Scope submitted to KISA describes that boundary in three parts:the organizational and operational perimeter: the Cloudflare entities, teams, and processes that operate the service;the infrastructure perimeter: the network and platform the certified service runs on;the information assets and personal information flows that fall inside the boundary under the ISMS control set.If a customer-consumed Cloudflare product is delivered through that certified service boundary, meaning it runs on the same certified platform, is operated by the same certified teams, and is governed by the same ISMS, it is covered by the certificate. The certificate is held by Cloudflare, Inc.That is a different shape from the reports most procurement teams work with. A SOC 2 report or an ISO 27001 certificate describes the system it covers and names the services included, so coverage is confirmed by finding the product in that list. The ISMS certificate carries no such list. Coverage follows the delivery path instead, whether or not a product is named anywhere.What this means for customersFor organizations operating in Korea, this gives legal, security, and procurement teams a local assurance benchmark alongside Cloudflare's broader compliance portfolio. ISO/IEC 27001 and SOC 2 demonstrate a general security posture. ISMS reflects Korea-specific legal and regulatory expectations. That distinction matters in third-party risk reviews and in preparing for a team’s own compliance assessments.Cloudflare’s entry can be found on KISA's public register of certified organizations, which is the independent, verifiable confirmation to cite in a risk review. Broader privacy and data protection material sits on the Cloudflare Trust Hub.The question that usually stalls a vendor review of Cloudflare is whether a particular product in use is in scope. The certificate does not answer that by name, because it lists no products. It answers by boundary, meaning that the product is in scope if it is delivered through the certified service.For multinational teams managing security across regions, the certification confirms that Cloudflare's program has been reviewed against local requirements in one of Asia's most important digital markets, not just designed for global scale.Building a better Internet, for everyoneISMS is not a harder certification than the other assurance audits we go through. It is a more nuanced one. It is built around the regulatory needs of one specific region, and it asks for genuine investment in understanding and embedding those needs, rather than mapping them onto a common control framework.Going through it made Cloudflare more global, not less. It pushed us to think carefully about what it means to serve users in a specific local context, with local language, local consent expectations, and local data protection requirements, and to put that into how the product behaves rather than only into a document.That is consistent with what we are working toward: helping build a better Internet for everyone, not just in the regions where regulatory requirements are straightforward, but everywhere.To learn more about Cloudflare's compliance and assurance programs, visit our Trust Hub.

title: [Cloudflare] Introducing full transaction detection for Cloudflare WAF
summary: Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation. It helps answer both "Does this request look malicious?" and "What happened when the application handled it?" Response rules can then block the origin’s response before it reaches the requester.These are valuable protections because the latest frontier models are uncovering vulnerabilities buried deep in widely used software, giving defenders clarity on what to fix — and attackers new paths to exploit. The recent php2shell vulnerability shows the stakes: a flaw in a common software component can put applications across the Internet at risk. AI agents scanning for vulnerabilities can be extremely persistent, adapting payloads using feedback, and chaining vulnerabilities, credentials, and permissions. An application's response can reveal whether an attempt worked and give an attacker information that helps them go deeper.Inspecting incoming requests remains essential for stopping recognizable attacks before they reach an application. But some threats become clear only when the request is considered alongside what the origin returns. A suspicious input followed by a response exposing sensitive information tells a different story from the same input followed by a rejection or an error.With these new capabilities, customers can use Cloudflare-managed protections or build their own policies combining request and response properties. This extends our always-on application security framework, with detection results available in Security Analytics to support investigation. Our first managed protections using this capability address the recently disclosed php2shell vulnerability.And the best part? We are making these new capabilities generally available to all Cloudflare customers, including Free plans.Request inspection is not enoughCloudflare WAF protects websites and APIs with managed rules, custom rules, and rate limiting. Managed rules provide protection for known attack techniques and vulnerabilities while custom rules let teams create their own policies using parameters such as an IP address, URL path, headers, and request body. These controls operate at the request level to stop exploits or unwanted traffic from reaching the origin.For many threats, this is the right place to act. However, treating every suspicious request as a confirmed exploit creates a difficult choice. Broad request signatures can catch more potential attacks, but they can also show “false positives”, such as matching legitimate traffic — which then breaks the applications. Deploying only rules that do not trigger false positives reduces that risk, but can leave more room for more ambiguous traffic to reach the server.The response provides the missing evidence. Cloudflare can now correlate it with the request that produced it, so detections can account for the outcome of the entire HTTP transaction.As an illustrative example, consider an application that lets users download files. An attacker manipulates the file parameter to request a private configuration file outside the permitted directory:GET /download?file=../../config/database.iniRequest inspection can recognize this path traversal attempt and block it before it reaches the application. The request alone, however, cannot establish whether the application would expose the file. It might reject the request, ignore the traversal, or return an error. If the request reaches the origin, a response like this provides additional evidence:200 OK Content-Type: text/plain  username=app_service password=EXAMPLE_SECRETFull transaction detection provides a missing piece: it can correlate the attempted file access with response content characteristic of a private configuration file. Configuration-like text can legitimately appear in documentation or example downloads; combining it with a traversal attempt provides stronger evidence of sensitive data exposure than either signal alone. A response rule can then replace the origin response with a Cloudflare WAF block page and HTTP 403 before it reaches the requester, effectively blocking the exploit by preventing sensitive information from reaching the attacker.Detection and mitigation are separate by designFull transaction detection extends the always-on detection framework we introduced earlier this year. Detections analyze traffic and attach metadata to the request and response, rules then decide what to do with those results.Separating those jobs gives customers visibility before they design a policy. Security teams can inspect detections in their own traffic, understand which endpoints and signatures are involved, and choose the response that fits their application. Similar to the approach for the request-based Attack Signature Detection, the outcome of the detections are stored in fields that can be accessed in the response custom rules or used in managed detections to block traffic.Mirroring the request detection fields, the following new fields are added to our platform:FieldDescriptioncf.waf.signature.response.confidenceConfidence values associated with matching signaturescf.waf.signature.response.categoriesCategories associated with matching signaturescf.waf.signature.response.refSignature reference IDs, up to 10The first full transaction detections focus on exploit confirmation for high profile vulnerability. It correlates suspicious input with response signals that indicate an exploit may have succeeded.We will expand coverage over time by supporting other use cases, including detecting data exposure and exfiltration signals. This is important for the Internet beyond any one application: defenses can distinguish probing from evidence of impact, while detection of exposed data and services can reach customers that do not have a dedicated security team tuning every WAF rule.Create rules on the responseDetecting evidence of exploitation is most useful if you can act on it in real time. Response custom rules turn full transaction detections into inline protection by blocking a matching origin response before it reaches the requester, although it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin.Security teams can now combine request and response properties with detection results to decide which responses to block. When a blocking rule matches, Cloudflare replaces the origin response with a WAF block page or a custom response.Response phase controls are available in the Cloudflare dashboard at the bottom of the Security > Security Rules page, with both managed protections and custom rules.We have released both managed and custom rules to all plans, including Free plans. Over time, we will follow the same approach we use for request detections, where managed detections for free plans focus on high-profile vulnerabilities, while paying customers get a richer catalog of detections.Managed detectionsAll customers get the protection of the full array of transaction detections through the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default ruleset, which is designed for a simple one-click deploy and simplified configurability. When a signature matches, the managed detection will block the response and return a standard WAF block page.You can edit the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default scope to run detections only on a portion of their applications, for example by excluding or restricting the detection to a specific path. Paying customers can use detection fields in custom response rules to create more tailored policies.Custom rulesCustom response rules are designed to give customers full control of the rule logic. A useful rule can stop an administration interface from being exposed when an authentication gateway has not marked the request as internal. For example:http.request.uri.path starts_with "/admin" and not http.request.headers eq "true" and http.response.code eq 200 and http.response.headers contains "text/html" This blocks only when an unauthenticated request targets `/admin` and the origin actually returns a successful HTML administration page. It does not block ordinary authentication failures, redirects, or non-administration traffic.All customers can create up to three custom response rules supporting Log and Block actions. The fields and functions available in response to custom rules mirrors what your plan gives you access to in request custom rules already. Creating rules on the response body is not yet available.Following the Attack Signature Detection approach, paying customers also have access to the outcome of attack detections through the cf.waf.signature.response.* fields listed above. These fields can be combined with other parameters (such as a hostname, URL path, source IP, request header) to enable protection on a single path, or limit the policy to application-specific context. We are currently rolling out the response fields to all our accounts. If you don’t have access to them yet, please contact your account team.Investigating matching requestsWhen a managed or custom response rule logs or blocks a transaction, the event is available in Security Events. This means responders can trace any detection back to the full context of the request and the specific rule that took action.At the moment, both request-only rules and full-transaction rules are shown together in the same analytics page. In Security Events, the events generated by response rules are part of the Managed Rules or Custom Rules service. You can filter events belonging to a specific rule ID in the relative rule list section.Get started todayFull transaction detection is generally available for all zones proxying traffic through Cloudflare. To verify that you’re protected, go to Security > Security Rules in the Cloudflare dashboard. If you want to customize your policy, start by reviewing full transaction detections in Security Analytics, then create the response phase policy that fits your application.

title: [Slack Engineering] Shipyard: How We Built Slack’s Next-Generation EC2 Platform
summary: Over the past few years, we’ve been on a journey to modernise how we run Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) instances at Slack. In our first post, Advancing Our Chef Infrastructure, we shared how we moved from a single Chef stack to a resilient, multi-stack setup with versioned cookbook deployments and safer promotion workflows. This afforded us far more reliability and operational control across tens of thousands of EC2 instances. Subsequently, in Advancing Our Chef Infrastructure: Safety Without Disruption, we tackled deployment risk without the need for teams to rewrite their cookbooks. By introducing split production environments, signal-based Chef runs, and smarter rollout mechanisms, we dramatically reduced the impact radius of failures while keeping our legacy platform stable. These changes allowed us to safely operate our EC2 ecosystem at scale while we plan the future at a relaxed pace. But as we kept improving, a bigger truth became clear. Even with safer rollouts, better orchestration, and stronger guardrails, the old model—continuously updating long-lived EC2 instances—was hitting its limits. Service-level deployments were tricky, infrastructure drift was inevitable, and coordinating changes across multiple layers added complexity. Containers solved this for some classes of workloads, but not everything could migrate easily. We needed a new approach—one that brought modern deployment practices like immutability, progressive rollouts, and automated safety directly to EC2 instances. Enter Shipyard. Shipyard is Slack’s next-generation EC2 platform. It treats infrastructure as deployable artifacts rather than endlessly mutable instances. It gives teams service-level deployment primitives, tight integration with our build and orchestration systems, and the confidence to update infrastructure with the same safety and predictability we expect from modern app delivery platforms. In this post—the third chapter of our journey—we’ll explain why we built Shipyard, the principles behind its design, and how it represents a fundamental shift in how we think about running EC2 instances at Slack. What Shipyard Provides Shipyard is designed to bring modern infrastructure principles to EC2 instances while preserving the flexibility teams expect from EC2. Rather than focusing on configuration management as the center of the system, Shipyard shifts responsibility toward build pipelines, deployable artifacts, and automated safety mechanisms. Some of the key capabilities of the platform include: Multi-Architecture and Multi-OS Support The platform is designed from the start to support multiple CPU architectures, including both AMD64 and ARM-based Graviton instances, with support for multiple operating systems such as Ubuntu, RHEL, and Amazon Linux. This flexibility allows teams to optimize for cost, performance, or compatibility without needing separate platform implementations. Shipyard is particularly valuable for workloads that cannot migrate to containers, such as infrastructure components, Kubernetes worker nodes, and our egress network stacks. Metrics-Driven Deployments with Safety Controls Each service integrates with our deployment orchestration system called Gondola to enable progressive rollouts with metric based automated safety checks. Deployments can automatically halt based on service health signals, or automated rollback to previous known good versions. Fast and Predictable Provisioning Shipyard uses a layered image approach, inspired by how containers work. A shared “golden” base image provides common infrastructure components, and service-specific images are built on top of that foundation. This minimizes work at launch time, so instances can come online quickly and predictably across regions. Simplified Configuration Management One of the biggest architectural shifts is how we use configuration management. Previously, instances would run scheduled Chef jobs that periodically checked and reapplied configuration, so any manual or unexpected changes would be reverted back to the desired state. In the new model, configuration is applied during well-defined lifecycle phases like image baking and initial provisioning, rather than being continuously enforced in the background. Configuration tools are mainly used to deploy services, not to constantly modify the entire system. This reduces background load, avoids unintended overwrites, and makes system behavior much easier to reason about, since instances aren’t continuously changing over time. Real-Time Inventory and Fleet Visibility Shipyard comes with a new inventory system called Peekaboo, giving us near real-time visibility into the state of our EC2 fleet. Instead of relying on Chef Server as the source of truth, Peekaboo taps directly into cloud events and instance metadata, providing better telemetry across environments. It can even track instances from non-Shipyard deployments, giving us a complete view of the entire fleet in one place. We built Peekaboo using AWS EventBridge, OpenSearch, and Lambda. It has everything teams need: a UI to explore the fleet, an API for integrations, and a command-line interface (CLI) for quick command-line checks. By centralising this information, it removes the guesswork and gives us a single place to view and manage EC2 instances. Short-Lived, Continuously Refreshed Instances To keep our EC2 instances secure and truly immutable, each instance has a limited lifespan and is automatically rotated on a regular schedule. This means our fleets are always fresh; potential vulnerabilities have less time to cause issues, and teams focus on replacing instances rather than making in-place changes. Golden Base Images: Introducing slack-zero At the foundation of the Shipyard is a shared base image called “slack-zero.” This is the core machine image built by Slack’s Compute Platform Team and maintained collaboratively with our security and monitoring teams. The slack-zero image contains: Operating system baseline and hardening Networking and service discovery configuration Monitoring and security agents Common tooling and foundational system configuration You can think of slack-zero similarly to how teams use a base Docker image or how we start from a vendor-supplied Ubuntu image and layer additional components on top. It provides a standardised, trusted foundation that every service inherits, while still allowing teams to customize their own runtime environment on top of it. Base images are treated as immutable but ephemeral. When foundational components need to change—such as a security patch, monitoring update, or networking improvement—a new slack-zero image is produced. Downstream service images can then rebuild on top of the updated base to inherit the latest fixes and improvements. To build slack-zero, we use AWS Image Builder rather than Packer. Image Builder provides several built-in advantages over our previous approach with Packer, including: Lifecycle Management: Old AMIs are automatically cleaned up using lifecycle policies, helping reduce storage costs. AWS System Manager (SSM) Parameter Publishing: Each new slack-zero image updates an SSM parameter that indicates the latest available AMI for an account. Service pipelines read this parameter to ensure they always build on the most up-to-date base. Event-Driven Automation: When a slack-zero image finishes baking successfully, EventBridge and Lambda automatically trigger downstream pipelines in service owner accounts so dependent images can be rebuilt. Built-in Testing: Before an AMI is published, Image Builder launches temporary instances and runs validation tests. This ensures every image is verified before distribution, reducing risk and increasing confidence in production rollouts. Together, these capabilities allow us to continuously evolve the platform foundation while keeping adoption friction low for service teams. Service Images Each service team builds its own AMIs using slack-zero as the foundation. This allows teams to control their runtime environment while inheriting standardized platform components maintained by the platform organization. Service image pipelines define: What software is installed How the service is configured What happens during instance initialisation for this service Because most configuration is baked directly into the image, instances launch quickly and consistently, minimizing configuration drift and ensuring predictable behavior across the fleet. By combining the immutable slack-zero base with service-specific layers, Shipyard provides both platform stability and team-level flexibility, enabling services to innovate safely without sacrificing operational consistency. Baking and Provisioning Shipyard separates instance preparation into two distinct phases: baking and provisioning. During the bake phase, we install packages and include configuration that is consistent across environments. This ensures every instance starts from a fully prepared, known-good state with the majority of work already completed before launch. Environment-specific settings—such as secrets, regional configuration, or deployment metadata—are applied during the provisioning phase when the instance boots. This step is intentionally lightweight and typically involves only dropping configuration, retrieving secrets, and starting services. By moving heavy operations like package installation into the bake phase, instances can become operational in seconds rather than minutes. This fast startup time is critical for scaling events, rolling deployments, and automated instance replacement. This provisioning model provides a strong balance of consistency, speed, and flexibility: images deliver a stable baseline, while minimal provisioning adapts instances to their runtime environment without introducing drift. Deployments and Fleet Updates When teams need to roll out changes, they build a new Amazon Machine Instance (AMI) and then run their deployment pipeline to roll it out. Instead of patching existing instances, fleets are updated through controlled replacements, keeping everything consistent and predictable. For Auto Scaling Groups (ASGs), we use AWS Instance Refresh, and Kubernetes worker fleets use Karpenter for lifecycle-driven updates. Services with special deployment needs can use alternative rollout executors. Our global deployment orchestrator, Gondola, supports these patterns, giving teams flexibility while keeping a consistent deployment experience. Emergency Fixes and Rapid Deployment Pathways For urgent situations, the platform allows targeted configuration changes on running instances, but these are meant for emergencies only. Affected instances are expected to be replaced afterward via regular deployment pipelines. Our emergency workflows use AWS Systems Manager with a predefined document to run selected Chef recipes, letting teams quickly apply critical fixes. Once stable, instances are cycled to return to the intended immutable state. What Do Customer Pipelines Look Like? Customer pipelines in Shipyard can have multiple stages, giving teams flexibility to design them around their service and operational needs. Each stage in Gondola represents a deployable unit, such as an ASG, a Kubernetes cluster, or a group of EC2 instances. For example, the Egress Team runs separate canary and production ASGs in each availability zone, with deployment stages ordered so updates flow sequentially. Gondola updates each stage, monitors key metrics, and rolls back automatically if problems are detected, preventing issues from spreading. This staged approach, combined with Shipyard’s fast provisioning and immutable AMIs, lets teams safely deploy complex updates at scale while maintaining observability and control. What Happens in the Gondola Stage? When Gondola builds an artifact, it produces a deployable package for a service with two main parts: The AMI to roll out across the fleet The Chef artifact containing versioned recipes associated with a Git commit Gondola treats these together as a single deployable unit. Each stage uses a service-defined executor to perform the rollout: ASG-based deployments: The executor updates the launch template with the new AMI and configuration. Chef code is packaged to Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3), and new instances use a baked-in bootstrapper to fetch the correct artifact and run the relevant recipes. Configuration metadata ensures only the right configuration is applied. Kubernetes worker fleets: The executor tells Karpenter which AMI to use and provides the same configuration metadata. Nodes bootstrap in the same way, ensuring consistent provisioning. For services with special deployment needs, Gondola makes it easy to add new executors. This lets Shipyard support different deployment models while keeping artifact handling and provisioning consistent and predictable. By combining AMI updates, versioned configuration artifacts, and metadata-driven bootstrapping, Gondola ensures every instance gets the correct software and configuration for its role, no matter how it’s deployed. Simple Pipeline Shared Responsibility Shipyard’s layered image model is built on a clear shared responsibility between platform teams and service teams. The Compute, Security, and Monitoring teams manage the base layer, making sure it includes all global infrastructure components, security patches, and essential configurations. Service teams then build their own AMIs on top of this base, adding the software and settings specific to their service. Whenever the Compute team rolls out a fix or update—whether it’s a security patch, a monitoring agent update, or a networking change—service teams are responsible for incorporating the updated base into their own AMIs. This way, every service image automatically benefits from the latest improvements and security fixes from the shared base. This approach lets each team focus on what they do best while keeping the fleet consistent, secure, and reliable. The diagram below illustrates how the base and service layers work together and highlights where each team’s responsibilities lie. A Caveat on Immutability While Shipyard instances are mostly immutable, there is an important exception: secrets. Each instance runs the Consul Template service, which allows us to roll out updated secrets from Vault without cycling the fleet. This means that, although packages and configurations are fixed at bake time, sensitive data like credentials or certificates can still be updated dynamically. Our infrastructure is semi-immutable: the core system and service layers remain consistent, but critical runtime secrets can be refreshed safely as needed. This approach balances stability, predictability, and security across the fleet. The Reaper The Reaper evaluates two primary inputs. First, it consumes signals from external systems—such as security tooling or AWS EC2 events—that indicate an instance may no longer be in its desired state and should be considered “tainted.” Second, The Reaper performs periodic checks to identify instances that have been running for longer than their allowed lifespan. When either condition is met, the instance is scheduled for replacement according to its service policies. This approach helps reduce configuration drift, limit exposure to vulnerabilities, and reinforce the principle that infrastructure should be updated by redeploying rather than modifying systems in place. The result is a platform that is more reliable, auditable, and predictable. For example, while manual remote access remains available for emergency scenarios, manually accessing a production-class node will generate a signal that marks the instance for eventual replacement, supporting our immutable infrastructure goals. The Reaper also integrates with Peekaboo to track instance age across the fleet. Once a node reaches its maximum lifespan, it follows the same graceful replacement workflow. Looking ahead, we plan to make the system more context-aware so that only meaningful changes—such as software updates or configuration drift—trigger replacement, while read-only or low-risk actions do not create unnecessary churn. Taming the Reaper The Reaper is designed not only to enforce lifecycle policies, but also to give teams control over how replacements occur. Built-in rate limiting allows service owners to define how many instances can be replaced at a time, scoped by service, region, or availability zone, preventing sudden capacity impacts. For emergency situations, we provide a global pause mechanism—the “big red button.” By placing a control object in S3, teams can temporarily halt all Reaper activity across the fleet. This provides a safe and immediate way to stop instance cycling during incidents or periods of elevated risk. We also provide a CLI that allows service owners to manage rate limits, inspect configuration, and activate or release the global pause when needed. In addition, controlled access mechanisms such as short-lived SSH certificate workflows can be used for break-glass scenarios where deeper investigation is required, while still maintaining overall lifecycle safety commitments. Together, these capabilities make the Reaper both predictable and controllable—enforcing instance immutability by default while giving teams the visibility and safeguards they need to operate confidently. How Do We Test Changes? Both platform teams and service owners need a safe way to test cookbook changes before merging a pull request, so we built a system called Ship Quick—a developer workflow that runs a realistic bake-and-provision test on real infrastructure. Developers run a CLI command from their cookbook repo, where a YAML file defines the test cases. Ship Quick packages the cookbook, uploads it to S3, and sends a workflow message to a queue. A fleet of worker instances—managed by a lightweight process called Longshoremen—picks up the job, detaches from its Auto Scaling Group, runs the Chef workflow, streams logs back to the CLI, and then terminates (unless the developer chooses to keep it for debugging). We run Longshorem in two separate worker fleets because of how our bootstrapping works. The vanilla Ubuntu fleet is used to bake and test the base slack-zero image—it can’t build on top of itself, so starting from a clean Ubuntu AMI is required. The slack-zero fleet is for service team cookbooks, which depend on the pre-baked slack-zero AMI. Running tests from this fleet ensures provisioning is validated against the same foundation used in production. Splitting the fleets this way helps ensure each layer is tested against the correct base. Both fleets scale automatically with demand, and slack-zero workers are continuously updated to the latest images so tests always reflect the current production environment. Teams that build images in their own AWS accounts can also provision dedicated worker fleets and route Ship Quick jobs to them, ensuring isolation while keeping the same workflow. What’s Next? So far, Shipyard has been working really well for short-lived services, and we’re actively onboarding teams from the legacy EC2 platform. Our next challenge is long-lived instances—things like Slack’s data nodes, singleton services like GitHub Enterprise, or third-party business technology instances such as Atlassian JIRA. These can’t be cycled quickly, so we need ways to patch and update them safely while ensuring the Reaper handles them correctly. We’re collaborating closely with service teams to develop new deploy executors in Gondola for these longer-lived workloads. As more teams adopt Shipyard, we’ll keep iterating on tooling, developer workflows, and the overall deployment experience to meet the platform’s diverse needs. Future posts in this series will cover the challenges we encounter as Shipyard evolves and take a closer look at its components—including the Shipyard API, image pipelines, developer workflows, and our inventory system. Stay tuned!

title: [Pulumi] Running Pulumi Neo in a Docker Sandbox: workshop recap
summary: The more an agent can do on its own, the more infrastructure work you can hand it, as long as its limits hold when it gets something wrong. In April, they didn’t hold for PocketOS. A coding agent on a routine staging task deleted the company’s production volume in 9 seconds. According to founder Jer Crane’s account, it used an API token it found in an unrelated file. Its explanation afterward: “I guessed that deleting a staging volume via the API would be scoped to staging only. I didn’t verify.” Railway recovered the data two days later. The agent had been told not to. “System prompts are advisory, not enforcing,” Crane wrote afterward. If the prompt can’t stop an agent, the limits have to sit where the agent can’t negotiate with them. That was the premise of Neo in a Docker Sandbox, the workshop Adam Gordon Bell and I ran with Mike Coleman from Docker. So we gave Pulumi Neo two layers. The first is a Docker Sandbox. Neo runs in its own microVM and reaches only the files and hosts we allow. The Pulumi token gets injected by a proxy on the way out, so Neo never holds the real credential. The second is Pulumi itself, which decides what Neo may change and when it has to ask. With both in place, you can let Neo work without approving every step. For why YOLO mode belongs in a sandbox at all, see my August post. Mike Coleman is a Principal Solutions Architect at Docker. His running joke is that agents “want to be helpful”. It happens in his own demos: Mike Coleman I talk to people about agents a lot. They just really want to please you. I don’t know how many times I’ve done a demo  governance for MCP servers, and I’ll be like, “Can you write to my Notion page?” And there will be a policy applied to the sandbox that says it can’t. But I have a connector enabled in Claude somewhere. And it’s like, “Well, not with that MCP server, but I can use this thing over here to do it.” Mike’s answer is to close those doors before the agent finds them: Mike Coleman The more you can create an environment where these alternate avenues are roadblocked, the safer you’re gonna be with agentic workflows. That’s where we’re coming at with the sandboxes: how do we take something that is as powerful as an agent, allow it to run as close to its full potential as possible, but avoid a bunch of catastrophic things. A deleted database scores the same as a failed task Adam’s explanation of why a capable agent does this starts with how it’s trained. Agents got good at code fast. METR measures the length of software task, in human hours, that a model can finish on its own half the time, and it has doubled every few months. Source: METR, Time Horizon 1.1. Behind that improvement is reinforcement learning on coding tasks. The model gets a task, tries it many times in a throwaway sandbox, and each attempt is scored pass or fail. Every attempt runs in a sandbox that resets afterward. In that sandbox, nothing it does can go worse than failing the task. There is no downside bigger than a zero, so the model never learns that some actions are worse than others. Adam Gordon Bell In the training environment, if you solve a task, you get one point. If you don’t solve the task, you get zero. But there’s no in-between. If you destroy the entire repo, if you delete prod, that’s the same thing. You got the task or you failed the task. There’s no asymmetric downside. Production is different. Adam Gordon Bell  existing benchmarks, no matter what you do, the worst you can get on any task is: you didn’t complete it. But in the real world, some tasks have a catastrophic downside. Published coding-agent training runs such as DeepSWE and SWE-Universe use that 1-or-0 reward. Adam’s answer is a matrix with reversibility on one axis and blast radius on the other. Training happens in the top row. Production work lives in the bottom right. Adam’s rule is that agents can act on their own when there are no side effects, when someone reviews the change, or when there’s an easy way to recover. The PocketOS agent was working in staging, which felt safe. The token it found let it leave staging without anyone noticing. Infrastructure as code moves production work toward those conditions. An agent’s change becomes a diff you can preview, check against policy, and review before it reaches the cloud. Six questions before an agent gets your cloud account Before an agent gets a cloud account, six questions: Engin Diri Who is this agent acting as? What is it allowed to change? And when does it stop and ask? That last one has a history. The human-in-the-loop pattern was very, very big at the start, and everybody was like, “Hey, there should always be a human approving stuff.” Then it shifted when everything came around to the Ralph loop, loop engineering and so on. Asking was considered something which slows you down. Still, maybe very important. Where does the agent actually run? Which credentials does it hold? And what stops it when it goes wrong? Keep these questions as a loose guardrail. Six questions before an agent gets a cloud account. Pulumi answers who, what, when, and what stops it. The sandbox answers where, and it splits the credentials question with Pulumi ESC (Environments, Secrets, and Configuration). Pulumi controls that live outside the prompt pulumi neo runs Neo in your terminal (Essentials, Pro, and Enterprise editions). Its controls live in Pulumi: Neo runs as you. It uses your pulumi login and role-based access control (RBAC) permissions, and its file and shell tool calls run locally, inside the sandbox. Approval mode sets when it asks. --approval-mode manual, the default, asks before every tool call, balanced only before pulumi up, and auto never. Read-only blocks Pulumi Cloud writes only. With --permission-mode read-only, Neo can’t trigger writes such as pulumi up, but it can still open ESC environments and reach the cloud accounts behind them. To keep it out of an environment, don’t grant your user or role environment:open on it. protect: true guards against accidental deletes. A deployment that would delete a protected resource fails. protect: false, pulumi state unprotect, or --ignore-protect still gets past it. Pulumi Policies blocks unsafe changes. Mandatory policies in a preventative policy group (Pro and Enterprise editions) run on every pulumi preview and pulumi up, Neo’s included, and stop a violating change before anything reaches the cloud. The workshop’s pack included s3-no-public-acl. Pulumi ESC replaces stored cloud keys. It mints short-lived AWS credentials through OpenID Connect (OIDC) for each run. They still reach the CLI, so they limit a leak’s damage rather than prevent it. What a Docker Sandbox isolates Each agent gets its own microVM, kernel, and Docker Engine. Only the workspace is mounted (plus a read-only skills store for supported agents), but SSH agent forwarding is on by default. All outbound TCP goes through a host proxy that injects proxy-managed credentials such as the Pulumi token. The sbx CLI and local sandboxes are free; centralized sandbox, network, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) controls are part of Docker’s paid AI Governance. What changed in Docker Sandboxes since August Secrets are global and reach running sandboxes. Since v0.38.0 (August 6), sbx secret set pulumi covers every sandbox whose kit asks for it. Since v0.45.0 (September 21), changing a global secret updates running sandboxes without a restart. Sandbox environment files (experimental). An sbxenv.yaml captures a sandbox’s agent, kits, workspace, ports, and credentials for sbx env run. Mike compared it to a dev container definition. Docker now says to keep the file under version control but outside the mounted workspace, because it can run host commands. Cloud sandboxes (experimental). sbx --cloud run claude runs the sandbox in Docker’s cloud, so it keeps going after you close the laptop. It needs sbx 0.45.0 or later and a pay-as-you-go Docker Agentic Platform subscription. New signups get a one-time $250 compute credit, instead of $25, through October 31, 2026. Running Neo inside a Docker Sandbox Every script is in the workshop repo. Store the token on the host, allow ghcr.io/dirien/ in kit.allowedSources, then start the sandbox from my kit plus a mixin for the demo’s AWS region: sbx secret set pulumi sbx run --name neo-demo --kit ./01-sandbox/region-kit \ ghcr.io/dirien/infrastructure-sandbox-kit:v0.10.0 ./02-app Neo isn’t a built-in sbx agent, so the sandbox opens a shell, where pulumi whoami -v works through the injected token while the variable holds a placeholder: echo "$PULUMI_ACCESS_TOKEN" proxy-managed From the host, the workshop’s boundaries.sh checks a host the kit doesn’t allow and one it does: sbx policy check network --sandbox neo-demo ifconfig.me sbx policy check network --sandbox neo-demo api.pulumi.com Under Balanced or Locked Down the first is denied, and sbx policy log neo-demo shows what the proxy refused. The Open preset allows all traffic. Without organization governance, a request that matches no rule is blocked and queued for your approval (sbx policy approval ls). The allow-list is an excerpt. Then start Neo: pulumi neo Inside the sandbox, I think auto approval mode is defensible for throwaway work. But allowed hosts, AWS included, still receive whatever Neo sends, and ESC’s short-lived credentials reach the CLI, so keep the Pulumi controls on. The last step, Neo trying to tear the stack down and protect: true refusing, didn’t make it into the live session. Where to start In an informal poll at the end of the workshop, 8 of the 11 people who voted said they don’t use a sandbox for their agents. If that’s you, start closed: pick Locked Down when the first start asks for a network preset. Read the denials in the terminal dashboard (sbx with no subcommand) or with sbx policy log, then approve them or add rules with sbx policy allow network <host>. On the Pulumi side, start Neo with balanced approval near production, so it works freely but asks before pulumi up, and back the stack with an ESC environment that uses OIDC. workshop virtual Neo in a Docker Sandbox: Using Pulumi’s Coding Agent for All Things Infra Safely and Securely 16 Sep Join Docker and Pulumi to run Neo, Pulumi’s infrastructure coding agent, inside a Docker Sandbox and turn plain-English requests into real cloud infrastructure. with Adam Gordon Bell, Engin Diri, Mike Coleman Beginner Register If you sandbox your agents differently, tell me how in the Pulumi Community Slack.

title: Railway's security incident is more serious than a normal outage. Customer environment variables may have been exposed.
summary: I've been following the Railway situation since the outage started, and things have gotten pretty concerning. I'm currently using Railway to host the backend of a small gaming marketplace I've been building. Like many developers, I initially thought this was another infrastructure outage affecting builds and deployments. But on October 21, Railway published a security disclosure confirming something much more serious. According to their statement, they detected anomalous activity involving systems responsible for storing customer environment variables. Their investigation suggests an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and, in some cases, obtained their decrypted contents. That's a serious concern for anyone hosting production applications on Railway. What Railway has disclosed so far Suspicious activity was detected in systems storing customer environment variables. An unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted secrets and obtained some decrypted values. The impact may be limited to a subset of customers, although the investigation is ongoing. Railway is recommending that all customers rotate their stored credentials, including API keys and database credentials. Deployments have been paused during the investigation. Railway believes the incident may be connected to a broader campaign targeting platform companies and AI inference providers. Railway has also started automatically rotating its bucket credentials and resetting certain integration credentials. As of the latest update I've seen, deployments remain paused. My biggest concern is how developers are supposed to rotate production credentials during an outage like this. Think about a small startup running its entire backend on Railway. You might have PostgreSQL credentials, JWT secrets, payment API keys, SMTP credentials, webhook secrets, and other sensitive information stored as environment variables. Now imagine being told that some of those credentials may have been exposed and that you should rotate everything immediately. That's obviously the correct security recommendation. But there's a problem. If you revoke your current database credentials or payment API keys before your running backend can use the replacements, you risk breaking critical functionality. And when deployments are paused, rolling out those changes becomes much more complicated. At the same time, leaving potentially compromised credentials active is also risky. For solo developers and small teams without dedicated infrastructure engineers, this is not a simple situation. What I've personally done so far I've reviewed my Railway account sessions, signed out older sessions, and inspected my existing environment-variable configuration. Everything appears normal from my side. But I understand that simply checking whether the variables still exist doesn't prove they weren't accessed. An attacker could potentially copy credentials without modifying anything visible in the dashboard. I haven't received confirmation that my particular project was affected, and I'm preparing to rotate my sensitive credentials carefully. The bigger issue is trust in managed infrastructure. One of the reasons developers use services like Railway is that they don't want to manage every part of their infrastructure manually. We trust these platforms to handle deployment infrastructure and provide secure storage for sensitive configuration. Of course, no platform can guarantee perfect security. But when the infrastructure responsible for storing customer secrets is potentially compromised, the impact can extend far beyond the hosting provider itself. A stolen database password could potentially allow unauthorized data access, depending on network restrictions and database permissions. A stolen API key could allow unauthorized operations or unexpected charges. A compromised authentication secret could potentially affect user sessions, depending on how the application implements authentication. None of this automatically means these things happened to Railway customers. These are potential consequences of exposed credentials. And that's exactly why the incident deserves serious attention. There are still several questions I'd like Railway to answer. What was the actual entry point used by the attacker? How could encrypted environment variables potentially be decrypted? Was this caused by compromised internal credentials, an infrastructure vulnerability, or something else? How many customers or projects were actually affected? Was there any evidence of attackers accessing customer databases directly? What time period should developers investigate when reviewing suspicious activity? What additional security measures will Railway introduce to prevent this from happening again? I appreciate that Railway disclosed the incident and started providing recovery guidance. But until the full scope is known, it's difficult for developers to understand their actual exposure. I'm curious how other Railway users are handling this. Have you already rotated all your production credentials? Have you noticed any unusual database activity, suspicious API calls, or unexpected service charges? Has Railway contacted you directly about your project being affected? Are you waiting for deployments to resume before rotating certain credentials, or have you temporarily disabled critical functionality? And probably the biggest question: Has this incident changed your trust in Railway, or do you still plan to keep your production applications there? I'm not trying to spread panic or suggest that every Railway project has been compromised. I'm sharing this because I'm running a real application on the platform, and I know other independent developers and small teams are in a similar position. I'd like to hear how others are approaching the security risks and what precautions they're taking. Hopefully, Railway publishes a detailed technical postmortem once the investigation is complete. submitted by /u/gramerscial

title: [Docker] Your Agent Runs in a Docker Sandbox. Now It Can Join a Team.
summary: Your sandboxed agents just got a team. The official BAND AI kit for Docker Sandboxes is now available at docker.io/bandhq/band-python-kit:latest. Docker Sandbox kits package everything an agent needs to run in a Docker Sandbox, so a single sbx create command gives you a ready-to-use agent environment. But an isolated agent is only half the story: real work means talking to people and to other agents. The BAND AI kit connects a sandboxed agent to the world. The agent runs on your machine with access to your repository, and joins a BAND room where it collaborates with humans and with agents running anywhere: locally, in the cloud, or on your own infrastructure. The same kit also connects sandboxes to each other, so multiple agents can work together in one room while each keeps its own isolated environment. In this post, we’ll show how a sandboxed agent connects to the world through BAND, using a local agent called Repo Doctor. BAND provides the collaboration layer for these agents. With BAND, developers can give agents persistent identities, bring them together in shared rooms, route work through @mentions, maintain message history, and surface tool execution events in the room. Each agent brings its own model, framework, tools, workspace, and infrastructure, and joins the room as a participant, wherever it runs. Docker Sandboxes give that agent an isolated microVM with its own kernel, filesystem, Docker daemon, and network. Inside it, the agent works with local source files, runs commands and tests, and makes changes to a mounted workspace. The BAND kit connects the two with one sbx create command. Humans (BAND Desktop) | v +------ BAND (cloud or self-hosted) ------+ | BAND API <--> Room --> Transcript | +-----------------------------------------+ ^ | REST + WebSocket | (opened from your machine) Your machine | +-------------|---------------------+ | Docker Sandbox microVM | | | | | mounted workspace | +-----------------------------------+ All connectivity is outbound. The agent opens a WebSocket to BAND and posts its replies through the BAND API, so nothing needs to reach into the sandbox. From the room’s point of view, it behaves like any other participant. Repo Doctor in a BAND room Here’s a neat example of how it all works together. Repo Doctor is a small agent that repairs a deliberately broken Python project. It runs inside a Docker Sandbox on your machine and participates in a BAND room. Wherever the agent actually runs, you give it work by mentioning its handle through the BAND platform: This example repo includes a band.yaml file that tells the BAND sbx kit which agent to launch. In this example, it points to main.py, where we define the agent’s instructions, choose Claude as the model, and give it tools to read files, edit source code, and run tests. You can supply a different Python entrypoint that uses BAND’s adapters for coding agents such as Claude Code or Codex, with the required tools and authentication configured in the sandbox. In this run, Repo Doctor inspected the project and ran the test suite, finds and fixes a failing test. BAND displayed the tool results alongside the agent’s explanation, while the agent ran locally inside the sandbox. Connect agents to BAND from your machine To try the same example, you’ll need Docker Sandboxes installed and signed in, a BAND account, and an Anthropic API key with API credits. You can adapt the example of course to your favorite technologies, but the simplest is to clone the example repository: git clone https://github.com/dockersamples/band-ai-sbx-demo.git cd band-ai-sbx-demo In BAND, create a remote agent or use an existing one. Note its handle, which you’ll use to mention it in a BAND room. Set agent.id in band.yaml to its agent UUID, and have its BAND API key ready for the next step. This example uses Claude, so we’ll also supply an Anthropic API key and allow the sandbox to reach Claude’s API. These settings follow from the agent implementation in main.py in the repo; the BAND kit itself does not require a particular model provider. The BAND agent key authenticates the connection to the platform. Store both keys before creating the sandbox. Each command prompts for a secret: enter the BAND agent key first, then your Anthropic API key. sbx secret set-custom \ --sandbox band-repo-doctor \ --host '**.band.ai' \ --env BAND_API_KEY \ --placeholder proxy-managed sbx secret set-custom \ --sandbox band-repo-doctor \ --host api.anthropic.com \ --env ANTHROPIC_PROXY_KEY \ --placeholder sk-ant-proxy-managed Docker Sandboxes keeps the real keys on the host and inserts them into outbound requests. The agent sees only placeholder values, and both credentials are scoped to this sandbox. Now create the sandbox with the BAND kit, allow the Claude API connection, and start the agent: sbx create --name band-repo-doctor \ docker.io/bandhq/band-python-kit:6.0.0 "$PWD" The kit already permits access to BAND and the Python package hosts. Add access to Claude’s API for this example: sbx policy allow network --sandbox band-repo-doctor api.anthropic.com Then start the agent in the prepared sandbox. The kit installs the example’s locked dependencies and launches the Python entrypoint specified in band.yaml. The agent connects to BAND, where you or other agents can communicate with it. sbx run --name band-repo-doctor Keep the terminal open while the agent runs. Once the log shows Connected to platform, add Repo Doctor to a BAND room and mention its handle like we did above. Create a room and add its participants: And then you or any other agents can issue commands via the BAND platform. A local agent in a larger BAND team Repo Doctor is a single-agent demo, but BAND rooms support larger arrangements. A room can contain agents running locally, in the cloud, or on your own infrastructure. They can mention each other, add specialists to a room, work sequentially or in parallel, and return the result to a human participant. For example, a planner agent can plan a change and ask a research agent to check the relevant API. When the work needs your repository, it mentions Repo Doctor. Only Repo Doctor needs access to the local workspace, so only that agent runs in the Docker Sandbox on your machine. After running the tests, Repo Doctor can @mention a reviewer with the result; the full execution events remain visible to the human in the room. The same pattern works across sandboxes: agents that each need their own isolated environment can run in separate sandboxes and still collaborate in the same room. BAND room |-- Planner agent (hosted) |-- Research agent (hosted) `-- @<your-user>/repo-doctor | v local Docker Sandbox | your workspace Humans can see the whole conversation. An agent’s context stays narrower because BAND delivers only messages that mention it. Hosted agents can collaborate broadly, with local execution attached to the one participant that actually needs it. BAND is particularly good at this composition. The local agent is one participant in a larger room, and its peers address it by handle. That saves you from building agent identity, routing, a worker connection back to the laptop, credential handling, and an audit trail before getting to the actual task. The seam between BAND and the sandbox is a WebSocket connection and a room mention, which is about as much integration code as I would like this problem to have. Getting started with BAND’s SBX Kit The BAND Python SDK repository contains the SDK and kit sources. The complete Repo Doctor example in the Docker Samples repository includes the agent, fixture, and scripts used to reproduce the screenshots. Create a sandbox from the published kit, connect the remote agent to a BAND room, and check sbx policy log to confirm its network requests match the policy you intended. For sandbox kit configuration, credentials, and network rules, see the Docker Sandboxes kit documentation.

title: [Sentry] We just gave a million dollars to Open Source maintainers
summary: The title is not a joke. For those of you who know Sentry, you know we've been giving back to Open Source maintainers since our early days in whatever ways we could. But around five years ago we really started to give in a more meaningful way. This year we increased our budget from $750,000 to $1,000,000. Why? Well, we know the obvious value of Open Source software and believe the companies who use it should support the people who build and maintain it. Open Source software is like the ultimate cheat code – shared libraries, frameworks, and tools that have years of community support and development that we can use off the shelf and focus time on building other products, services, and businesses. Sentry benefits from this every day. Funding these projects and maintainers keeps the flywheel going. LLMs have extended what we can build with these tools. But the AI stack also depends on Open Source. That's one reason why we added NumFOCUS to the foundations we supported in 2025 and continue to support this year too. (The more you know: NumFOCUS is a nonprofit that helps fund the Open Source scientific computing tools used in today's AI development.) The Open Source Pledge All this said, Sentry is not alone. This October marks the second anniversary of the Open Source Pledge, an initiative we started to help recognize companies who felt the same way we did and highlight Open Source maintainers. As of today, the Pledge's 37 member companies have paid a total of $8,421,535 to Open Source maintainers and foundations. We also started the Open Source Pledge because, to put it bluntly, we don't believe in freeloading. Here's a little PSA on why you should join the Pledge. Just two months ago in August, the Python Software Foundation (PSF) shared that its AWS spend had increased by ~69% from July of previous year. This shouldn't be a surprise to us because our prompt-engineered applications are driving more Python development, agents are installing packages, and more CI runs are all contributing to the demand on registries. The PSF also highlighted the need for more funding to grow the team operating this infrastructure. Our ask: Consider giving back and join the Open Source Pledge, it's easy. How did we distribute the $1,000,000? We sent $495,000 to thanks.dev for them to distribute to hundreds of maintainers whose packages we use.
